category.name: Parallel Programming
category.description: Threads, processes, async I/O, synchronisation, hardware and distributed systems.

questions.text: A _ contains one or more ___.
options: process; threads
thread; processes
thread; other threads
process; other processes
questions.explanation: A thread is a path of execution inside a process, and every process has at least one thread. Child processes are separate processes, not parts of their parent.

questions.text: Which statement best distinguishes concurrency from parallelism?
options: Concurrency means tasks overlap in time; parallelism means they execute at the same instant
Concurrency requires multiple cores; parallelism can be achieved on a single core
Concurrency applies to I/O work; parallelism applies only to network work
Concurrency and parallelism are two names for the same execution model
questions.explanation: Concurrent tasks are all in progress over the same period, possibly by taking turns. Parallel tasks actually run simultaneously, which needs hardware such as multiple cores.

questions.text: On a single-core CPU without simultaneous multithreading, how can two tasks run?
options: In parallel, executing at the same instant
Only sequentially, one finishing before the other starts
Concurrently, by taking turns on the core
Only if both tasks are separate processes
questions.explanation: The scheduler can switch between the tasks so both make progress, which is concurrency. Executing both at the same instant (parallelism) needs more than one hardware execution context.

questions.text: What does parallel execution require that concurrent execution does not?
options: An event loop that switches between pending tasks
Hardware that can run several operations at once
Tasks written with async/await so they can yield
A shared address space so the tasks can exchange data
questions.explanation: Concurrency can be achieved by interleaving tasks on one core. Parallelism needs multiple execution resources, such as several CPU cores, so work truly runs simultaneously.

questions.text: Two threads each make a blocking, synchronous HTTP request, and their waits for the responses overlap. How is this program best described?
options: Sequential, because each call blocks until its response arrives
Concurrent, even though each individual call is synchronous
Asynchronous, because two threads are involved
Parallel only if the responses arrive at exactly the same instant
questions.explanation: Synchronous describes how each caller waits; concurrency describes whether several tasks are in progress over the same period. Here both requests are in progress at once, so the program is concurrent.

questions.text: A program reads two independent files and then combines their contents. Which ordering constraint must it respect?
options: The first file must be read completely before the second read starts
Both reads must run in parallel on separate cores
The combine step can start as soon as either read finishes
Both reads must finish before combining; the reads may run in any order
questions.explanation: Independent tasks can be reordered or overlapped, but a dependent step must wait for every result it uses. This is non-sequential execution with one dependency.

questions.text: A program starts threads A, B and C in that order. In which order are they guaranteed to run?
options: A, then B, then C, matching the creation order
No particular order; the scheduler decides
C, then B, then A, because the newest thread runs first
In order of their thread IDs, lowest first
questions.explanation: Thread scheduling is nondeterministic. If the order matters, it must be enforced with synchronization such as joins, events or condition variables.

questions.text: Which of these does each thread in a process have its own copy of?
options: Its call stack
The heap
Global and static variables
The table of open files
questions.explanation: Threads share the process's code, data, heap and open files. Each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter so it can follow its own path of execution.

questions.text: Compared with threads, processes _____.
options: require more overhead to create
are simpler to communicate between
are considered more "lightweight"
are faster to switch between
questions.explanation: Creating a process means setting up a separate address space and other resources. Threads reuse their process's memory, so they are cheaper to create and switch between.

questions.text: Two processes need to exchange data. What do they normally use?
options: Ordinary global variables, since the OS shares them automatically
An IPC mechanism such as a pipe, socket or shared memory
Thread-local storage, which the OS makes visible to every process
The process table, which stores each process's variables
questions.explanation: Processes have separate address spaces and cannot read each other's memory directly. They communicate through IPC mechanisms that the operating system provides.

questions.text: The operating system assigns each process a unique _____.
options: CPU core for its whole lifetime
process name
process identifier (PID)
number of threads
questions.explanation: The PID lets the OS track and manage each process. Several processes can share a name, and processes are not tied to one core unless affinity is set.

questions.text: A thread is waiting for data to arrive from a network socket. Which scheduling state is it in?
options: Ready
Running
Terminated
Waiting
questions.explanation: A waiting (blocked) thread cannot continue until an event occurs, such as input arriving. A ready thread could run immediately and is only waiting for CPU time.

questions.text: In a process with two kernel-scheduled threads, thread 1 blocks in a read() on a socket. What can thread 2 do meanwhile?
options: Keep running, because blocking affects only the calling thread
Nothing, because a blocking call suspends every thread in the process
Run only after the OS converts the read into a nonblocking call
Run only if it belongs to a different process
questions.explanation: Scheduling states apply to individual threads. While thread 1 waits for data, thread 2 is still ready or running, which is how threads overlap I/O with other work.

questions.text: A process is paused at a breakpoint by a debugger. Which description fits its state?
options: Waiting, exactly like a process blocked on disk I/O
Zombie, because it is no longer executing
Stopped, a suspension distinct from waiting for an event
Ready, because it could run as soon as a core is free
questions.explanation: A stopped process will not run until it is explicitly resumed, for example with SIGCONT, even if CPU time is available. A blocked process resumes when its event occurs, and a zombie has already terminated.

questions.text: What characterises an asynchronous call compared with a synchronous one?
options: It always runs the operation on another CPU core
The caller can continue and handle the result or error later
It returns its result before the operation starts
It prevents any other thread from running meanwhile
questions.explanation: An asynchronous call lets the caller start work and receive the result later, for example via a future, callback or await. It does not by itself imply another core or thread.

questions.text: An async program starts a download and awaits it before starting the next one, for ten files. How do the downloads run?
options: In parallel on separate cores
Concurrently, all ten overlapping
Sequentially, one after another
In a random order chosen by the event loop
questions.explanation: Using async syntax does not create overlap by itself. Each download is awaited to completion before the next is started, so they still happen one at a time.

questions.text: A program calls a nonblocking read on a socket that has no data available. What happens?
options: The thread sleeps until the kernel signals that data arrived
The OS raises a fatal error and terminates the process
The call waits for a fixed timeout and then retries
It returns at once, reporting that no data is ready
questions.explanation: On POSIX, read() on an O_NONBLOCK socket fails with EAGAIN instead of sleeping. The program must retry later or ask for a readiness notification, whereas a blocking read would wait for data.

questions.text: A program downloads 100 files one after another and spends most of its time waiting for responses. Which change is most likely to speed it up?
options: Buying a CPU with a higher clock speed
Overlapping the requests with async I/O or threads
Rewriting the parsing code with a faster algorithm
Splitting each file's checksum calculation across cores
questions.explanation: The program is I/O-bound, so its time goes into waiting. Overlapping independent requests hides that waiting; faster computation helps little when the CPU is mostly idle.

questions.text: A downloader that overlaps its requests stops getting faster beyond 20 concurrent requests, while its CPU usage stays low. What is the most likely limit?
options: The CPU, because one core cannot issue more than 20 requests
The event loop, which cannot track more than 20 tasks
The network link or the remote server, which is now saturated
The operating system's limit of 20 threads per process
questions.explanation: Overlapping hides waiting, but the disk, network or remote service still caps how much I/O can complete per second. Once that resource is saturated, more concurrency adds no throughput.

questions.text: A single-threaded calculation keeps one of eight cores at 100% while total CPU usage shows about 12%. What kind of task is it?
options: CPU-bound, because the one core it uses is saturated
I/O-bound, because overall CPU usage is low
Memory-bound, because the CPU is not fully used
Idle, because most cores have no work
questions.explanation: A task is CPU-bound when computation limits its speed. Using only one core can make total utilisation look low even though that core is fully busy.

questions.text: A 10-millisecond calculation is split into 8 pieces on 8 cores, and the program becomes slower. What is the most likely cause?
options: Creating, coordinating and joining the workers costs more than the work saved
Parallel code always runs slower than sequential code
The CPU lowers its clock speed whenever more than one core is busy
The pieces must run one after another because they share a process
questions.explanation: Parallelism has overhead for starting workers, distributing data and combining results. For small amounts of work that overhead can outweigh the speedup, so measure before parallelising.

questions.text: A server moves from one core to four, handling four independent requests at the same time. What does parallelism mainly improve here?
options: The time each individual request takes from start to finish
Throughput, the number of requests completed per second
The amount of memory each request needs
The order in which the requests are completed
questions.explanation: Running independent requests simultaneously completes more work per unit of time. A single request still runs on one core, so its own latency is not reduced.

questions.text: A race condition _____ a data race.
options: only occurs when there is
can occur independently of
is just another name for
is always caused by
questions.explanation: A race condition is a logic error where correctness depends on timing or ordering. It can happen even when every access is properly locked, so no data race exists.

questions.text:
Two threads run buyer() while tickets starts at 1. Each access holds the mutex. What is wrong?

std::mutex m;
int tickets = 1;

bool available() { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m); return tickets > 0; }
void take()      { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m); --tickets; }

void buyer() {
    if (available()) take();
}
options: Nothing, because every access to tickets is protected by the mutex
It deadlocks, because take() locks a mutex that available() still holds
It has a data race, so the C++ program has undefined behavior
Both threads can pass the check before either takes, leaving tickets at -1
questions.explanation: There is no data race, since every access is locked, but the check and the update are separate critical sections. This check-then-act race condition is fixed by holding one lock across both steps.

questions.text: Which situation is a data race?
options: Two threads read the same shared variable at the same time
A single-threaded program competes with other processes for CPU time
One thread writes a shared variable as another reads it, unsynchronized
Several threads wait on the same condition variable for a signal
questions.explanation: A data race needs concurrent accesses to the same location, at least one of them a write, without proper synchronization. Concurrent reads alone are safe.

questions.text: Why can a program with a race condition produce different results on different runs?
options: The CPU randomly corrupts values held in shared memory
The compiler generates different code on every run
Threads run more slowly when the network is busy
The interleaving of thread operations can differ each run
questions.explanation: Thread interleaving depends on scheduling, load and timing, which vary between runs. When correctness depends on that order, the output changes with it.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of synchronization in concurrent programming?
options: To coordinate shared access and ordering between tasks
To make concurrent programs run faster on more cores
To reduce the memory each thread needs for its stack
To improve the CPU's cache hit rate for shared data
questions.explanation: Synchronization primitives such as mutexes, semaphores and condition variables prevent conflicting accesses and enforce ordering. They add overhead, so they rarely make code faster.

questions.text: What does "mutual exclusion" guarantee?
options: Each thread receives an equal share of CPU time from the scheduler
Two processes never share any memory pages with each other
A thread can never be preempted by the scheduler
Only one thread at a time executes a protected critical section
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion, typically provided by a mutex, lets only one thread at a time enter the protected code. Others trying to enter must wait until it is released.

questions.text: What is a critical section?
options: Code accessing shared state that must not run in several threads at once
The main function, where every thread of the program starts
Code that must run faster than the rest of the program
Code that handles fatal errors before the program exits
questions.explanation: A critical section touches shared mutable state, so concurrent execution could corrupt it. It is protected with a lock and should be kept as short as possible.

questions.text: What does it mean for code to be thread-safe?
options: It runs only on a single dedicated thread chosen by the OS
It never raises exceptions, whichever thread calls it
It stays correct when called from several threads at once
It always runs at a higher priority than other code
questions.explanation: Thread-safe code protects or avoids shared mutable state, so concurrent calls do not corrupt data or break its invariants.

questions.text: What is a deadlock?
options: A thread that runs in an infinite loop and never yields
Threads each waiting forever for a resource another one holds
A memory leak caused by threads that are never joined
A crash caused by one thread accessing memory another freed
questions.explanation: In a deadlock the threads are all blocked waiting on each other in a cycle. Nothing breaks the cycle, so they wait forever.

questions.text: Which conditions must all hold at the same time for a deadlock to occur?
options: Mutual exclusion, preemption, starvation, and busy waiting
Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait
Circular wait, priority inversion, preemption, and livelock
Shared memory, multiple cores, preemption, and blocking I/O
questions.explanation: These are the four Coffman conditions. Breaking any one of them, for example circular wait by acquiring locks in a global order, prevents deadlock.

questions.text: What is starvation?
options: A thread that consumes so much memory that others cannot run
A worker thread that has no more tasks left in its queue
All threads blocked waiting for each other in a cycle
A thread repeatedly denied a resource while others keep using it
questions.explanation: A starving thread could run but keeps losing out, for example to higher-priority threads or a stream of readers. Unlike deadlock, the rest of the system keeps making progress.

questions.text: What is priority inversion?
options: A high-priority task waiting on a resource held by a low-priority task
The scheduler deliberately running low-priority tasks first
Two tasks swapping their priorities after every time slice
A task's priority value being stored in memory with the wrong sign
questions.explanation: If the low-priority holder is itself preempted by medium-priority work, the high-priority task can wait a long time. Priority inheritance is a common fix.

questions.text: What is a context switch?
options: Switching a program from one programming language to another
Moving a thread's data from the heap onto its own stack
Saving one thread's state and restoring another's so it can run on the CPU
Changing the scheduling priority of a thread that is running
questions.explanation: The scheduler saves registers, the program counter and other state of the current thread, then loads another's. Switching between processes also changes the address space, which costs more.

questions.text: What is the difference between preemptive and cooperative multitasking?
options: Preemptive runs only on multicore CPUs; cooperative runs only on single-core CPUs
Preemptive is used for I/O-bound work; cooperative is used for CPU-bound work
Preemptive lets the scheduler interrupt a task; cooperative relies on tasks to yield voluntarily
Preemptive requires separate processes; cooperative requires threads in one process
questions.explanation: OS threads are usually preempted when their time slice ends. Coroutines in an event loop are cooperative: they switch only when a task yields, for example at an await.

questions.text: What makes an operation atomic?
options: It compiles to exactly one machine instruction
It always finishes in constant time
It can never fail or raise an error
Other threads can never observe it partially completed
questions.explanation: An atomic operation is indivisible from other threads' point of view: they see either the state before or after it. It is not necessarily a single instruction or fast.

questions.text: What does a memory model define in concurrent programming?
options: The physical layout of RAM modules and channels on the motherboard
Rules for when, and in what order, writes become visible to other threads
The algorithm the allocator uses to place objects on the heap
The maximum amount of stack and heap memory a thread may use
questions.explanation: Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations. A language memory model, such as C++'s, states which orderings and visibility guarantees synchronization operations provide.

questions.text: What does a happens-before relationship between operation A and operation B guarantee?
options: A appears earlier than B in the source code
A and B run on the same CPU core
The effects of A are visible to B
A finishes executing within one time slice of B
questions.explanation: Happens-before is established by synchronization, such as unlocking and then locking the same mutex. Source order alone does not create it across threads.

questions.text:
In this C++ program, is main guaranteed to print 1?

int x = 0;

int main() {
    std::thread t([] { x = 1; });
    t.join();
    std::cout << x << '\n';
}
options: No, x must be std::atomic<int> for the write to become visible
No, the program has a data race on x
Only on x86, which keeps stores in program order
Yes, the thread's completion happens before join() returns
questions.explanation: The end of a thread synchronizes with the return of join(), so the write to x happens before the read and there is no data race. ThreadSanitizer reports nothing for this program.

questions.text: A concurrent program is deterministic when it _____.
options: always takes exactly the same time to run on a given machine
uses a fixed number of threads chosen at start-up
gives the same result for the same input under any scheduling
cannot be preempted or interrupted by the operating system
questions.explanation: Determinism concerns results, not timing. A deterministic concurrent program enforces every ordering its output depends on, so different interleavings give the same answer.

questions.text: In Python's threading module, which call lets a thread sleep until another thread notifies it?
options: Condition.wait()
Lock.acquire()
Thread.join()
time.sleep()
questions.explanation: Condition.wait() releases the condition's lock and blocks until notify() or notify_all() is called. join() waits for a thread to finish, not for a notification.

questions.text: Why should a consumer use condition.wait_for(predicate) (or re-check its condition in a loop) rather than a single condition.wait()?
options: wait() returns immediately unless a predicate is passed
wait_for() keeps the lock held while sleeping, so no other thread can interfere
When it wakes up, the shared state may no longer satisfy its condition
wait() can only be woken by notify_all(), never by notify()
questions.explanation: Another thread may consume the item first, or the wakeup may be spurious. Checking the predicate while holding the lock after every wakeup keeps the consumer correct.

questions.text: A Python thread calls cond.wait() on a threading.Condition without first acquiring it. What happens?
options: It acquires the lock automatically and then waits
It waits normally, because the lock is only needed for notify()
It returns False immediately
RuntimeError is raised, because the lock is not held
questions.explanation: wait() must release the condition's lock while sleeping and reacquire it afterwards, so the caller has to own it; Python raises RuntimeError: cannot wait on un-acquired lock.

questions.text: Several Python threads run counter += 1 on a shared global. How do you make the update reliably thread-safe?
options: Rely on the GIL, since counter += 1 is a single atomic step
Wrap the update in with lock: using one shared threading.Lock
Declare counter as global inside every thread function
Set a threading.Event before each update
questions.explanation: counter += 1 compiles to separate load, add and store bytecodes, and the GIL is not a synchronization guarantee for that sequence. A shared Lock makes the whole update mutually exclusive.

questions.text: On CPython 3.12, four threads each run counter += 1 200,000 times, and every test run prints 800000. What does this show?
options: The GIL makes += on a global atomic in every CPython version
Python guarantees that integer updates are thread-safe
Nothing reliable: the result relies on interpreter details, so it still needs a lock
Threads in CPython 3.12 never switch in the middle of a function
questions.explanation: In 3.12 a thread switch rarely lands inside that short sequence, so lost updates are uncommon but not ruled out. The language promises nothing, and the optional free-threaded build (3.13+) runs the threads truly in parallel.

questions.text: Why do Python threads rarely speed up CPU-bound pure-Python code in CPython 3.12?
options: Python threads are always scheduled on the same core as the main thread
The GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time
Each Python thread is limited to a fixed share of CPU time
CPython runs threads one after another, never interleaving them
questions.explanation: CPU-bound threads take turns holding the GIL, so they gain little or nothing. Processes or native code that releases the GIL give parallelism; CPython 3.13 adds an optional free-threaded build without a GIL.

questions.text: Which situation is the best use case for a C++ std::shared_mutex?
options: Many threads read a shared value, but only a few modify it
Many threads modify a shared value, but only a few read it
Only a few threads both read and modify a shared value
Every thread needs exclusive access to the value
questions.explanation: A shared_mutex lets many readers hold shared ownership at once, while a writer takes exclusive ownership. It pays off when reads greatly outnumber writes.

questions.text:
The main thread holds m in shared mode. What does this C++ code print?

std::shared_mutex m;
m.lock_shared();
bool w = true, r = false;
std::thread t([&] {
    w = m.try_lock();
    r = m.try_lock_shared();
    if (r) m.unlock_shared();
});
t.join();
std::cout << w << ' ' << r << '\n';
options: 1 1
1 0
0 1
0 0
questions.explanation: Exclusive ownership needs every reader to leave, so try_lock() fails. Shared ownership can be held by many threads at once, so the second reader's try_lock_shared() succeeds.

questions.text: Why would you mark a Python background thread as a daemon thread?
options: Daemon threads always run at the lowest scheduling priority
Daemon threads are restarted automatically by the interpreter if they crash
Daemon threads run in a separate process, so they bypass the GIL
A daemon thread does not keep the program alive when the main thread finishes
questions.explanation: The interpreter waits for non-daemon threads at shutdown but not for daemon threads. Daemons suit best-effort work, such as a heartbeat, that can be abandoned at exit. Set daemon=True; setDaemon() is deprecated.

questions.text: Why is it risky to write important log records from a daemon thread?
options: It may be stopped abruptly at exit, losing the last writes
Daemon threads are not allowed to open files for writing
Every record a daemon writes is duplicated in the log
Daemon threads run without the process's file permissions
questions.explanation: Daemon threads are stopped without cleanup when the interpreter exits, so buffers may never be flushed. Important work should use a non-daemon thread with a stop signal and join().

questions.text: A Python thread's target raises ZeroDivisionError. What happens when the main thread calls t.join()?
options: join() re-raises the ZeroDivisionError in the main thread
join() returns None; the traceback was printed by the thread
join() blocks forever because the thread did not finish normally
The whole process exits with the thread's exception
questions.explanation: An uncaught exception ends only that thread and is reported through threading.excepthook. To pass errors back, catch them in the thread or use concurrent.futures, whose result() re-raises.

questions.text: In C++, what happens right after a std::thread object is constructed with a callable?
options: It starts running the callable, subject to OS scheduling
The thread waits until the parent calls start()
The thread waits until the parent calls join()
The thread stays idle until detach() is called
questions.explanation: std::thread has no start() method; construction launches the thread. join() and detach() only decide how its lifetime is managed.

questions.text:
Why does this C++ program fail to compile, and what fixes it?

void add_one(int& x) { ++x; }

int main() {
    int v = 0;
    std::thread t(add_one, v);
    t.join();
}
options: Arguments are copied and passed as rvalues, so pass std::ref(v)
std::thread cannot run free functions; wrap add_one in a lambda
v must be global, because threads cannot use local variables
add_one must return a value; change it to return int
questions.explanation: std::thread stores decayed copies of its arguments, which cannot bind to int&, so a static assertion fails. With std::ref(v) the thread changes v, which must outlive the thread.

questions.text: What happens if a std::thread object is destroyed while it is still joinable?
options: The thread is detached automatically
The destructor joins the thread automatically
The thread is cancelled at its next blocking call
The program calls std::terminate
questions.explanation: Destroying a joinable std::thread is treated as an error, so the program terminates. Every std::thread must be joined or detached first, or use std::jthread.

questions.text: What does std::jthread (C++20) do in its destructor if the thread is still joinable?
options: It detaches the thread and returns immediately without waiting
It requests a stop through its stop token and then joins the thread
It calls std::terminate, exactly like std::thread
It forcibly kills the thread without waiting for it to finish
questions.explanation: std::jthread calls request_stop() and then join(). The thread function can watch its std::stop_token to exit promptly, which makes RAII-style cleanup safe.

questions.text: In C++, after calling t.detach(), what does t.joinable() return?
options: true
true until the detached thread finishes
It throws std::system_error
false
questions.explanation: Detaching disassociates the thread from the std::thread object, so the object no longer represents a thread and cannot be joined.

questions.text:
What does this C++ program print?

thread_local int n = 0;
std::mutex m;

void work() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) ++n;
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
    std::cout << n << '\n';
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join(); b.join();
    std::cout << "main " << n << '\n';
}
options: 3, 6, then main 6
3, 3, then main 0
3, 3, then main 6
The output is unpredictable because of a data race on n
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own n, so each counts to 3 and no data race occurs. The main thread's copy is never incremented and stays 0.

questions.text: What does a barrier guarantee for a group of threads?
options: No thread passes it until all participants have arrived
Only one thread at a time can pass the barrier
Operations before the barrier execute as one atomic step
Threads resume in the order in which they arrived
questions.explanation: A barrier is a meeting point. Each thread waits there until the required number of threads arrive, which controls the relative order of the phases before and after it.

questions.text: In Python, a thread must finish a section of code before other threads pass a threading.Barrier. It should call the barrier's _ method ___ executing that code.
options: wait(); before
wait(); after
notify_all(); after
release(); before
questions.explanation: Calling wait() after the code means the thread reaches the meeting point only once its work is done. No participant passes the barrier until all have called wait().

questions.text: Workers must all finish phase $k$ before any of them starts phase $k + 1$, and this repeats 100 times. Which C++20 primitive fits best?
options: std::barrier, calling arrive_and_wait() after each phase
std::latch, with each worker calling count_down() per phase
std::counting_semaphore, acquired at the start of each phase
std::recursive_mutex, locked by each worker around each phase
questions.explanation: A std::barrier resets automatically after each phase, so it suits repeated phases. A std::latch can be used only once.

questions.text: The main thread must wait once until 5 worker threads have finished their initialization; the workers then carry on. Which C++20 primitive fits best?
options: std::barrier with a completion function
std::shared_mutex held in shared mode by each worker
std::condition_variable with no predicate
std::latch(5): workers call count_down(), main calls wait()
questions.explanation: A latch is a single-use countdown: the waiter is released once the count reaches zero, and the workers do not have to wait for each other.

questions.text: In C++, a thread has locked a std::recursive_mutex three times. How many times must it unlock it before another thread can acquire it?
options: Once
Twice
Three times, once per lock
None, because other threads can share it
questions.explanation: A recursive mutex keeps an ownership count for the owning thread. It becomes available to other threads only when the count returns to zero.

questions.text: A function holds a threading.Lock and calls a helper that acquires the same lock in the same thread. What happens?
options: The helper acquires the lock again because the same thread owns it
The thread blocks forever, because Lock is not reentrant
Python raises RuntimeError immediately
The first acquisition is released automatically
questions.explanation: A plain Lock has no owner tracking, so a second acquire() waits forever. An RLock lets its owning thread acquire it repeatedly, as long as it releases it the same number of times.

questions.text: In C++, what does try_lock() do when the mutex is already locked by another thread?
options: Blocks until the mutex becomes available, then returns true
Keeps retrying in a loop until it succeeds
Returns false immediately without blocking
Throws an exception describing the owner
questions.explanation: try_lock() never waits, so the caller can do other work or back off. It may even fail spuriously when the mutex is free, and it gives no fairness guarantee.

questions.text: A thread that already owns a std::mutex calls lock() on it again. What does the C++ standard say happens?
options: The second call succeeds and increments an ownership count
The second call returns immediately without doing anything
The second call always throws std::system_error
The behavior is undefined; in practice it often deadlocks
questions.explanation: std::mutex is not recursive, and locking it while already owning it violates a precondition. Use std::recursive_mutex, or restructure the code so the lock is taken once.

questions.text: Why would ThreadA call join() on ThreadB?
options: So that ThreadB waits until ThreadA has terminated
So that ThreadA waits until ThreadB has terminated
To wake ThreadB up if it is blocked
To terminate ThreadB immediately
questions.explanation: join() blocks the calling thread until the target thread finishes, for example before ThreadA uses ThreadB's results. It never stops or wakes the target.

questions.text: When would you call a condition variable's notify_one() instead of notify_all()?
options: When a specific, named waiting thread must wake up
When every waiting thread must re-check the condition
When no thread is currently waiting on it
When any single waiter can handle the change
questions.explanation: notify_one() wakes a single, unspecified waiter, for example when one item has been added to a queue. Waking everyone would make the rest compete and go back to sleep.

questions.text: What should a thread do before notifying a condition variable?
options: Update the shared state while holding the associated mutex
Notify first, then lock the mutex and update the state
Wait on the same condition variable to check that someone is listening
Update the state without the mutex, because notification provides the ordering
questions.explanation: Waiters check a predicate under the mutex, so the state change must also be made under it. The notification can be sent before or after unlocking; changing state unlocked risks missed wakeups.

questions.text: Which is a common use case for a counting semaphore?
options: Counting how many threads the program has created
Measuring how long a program has been running
Limiting concurrent use of a pool of identical resources
Recording the order in which threads started
questions.explanation: The count represents available resources, such as database connections. Acquiring takes one slot, releasing returns it, and threads wait when none are free.

questions.text: A threading.Semaphore(3) guards code that appends to a shared Python list. Is the list protected from concurrent modification?
options: No, up to three threads can be inside at once, so the list needs its own lock
Yes, a semaphore always provides mutual exclusion
Yes, because a semaphore count above one makes it a reader-writer lock
No, because semaphores can only be used between processes
questions.explanation: A count above one deliberately lets several threads in at the same time. It limits concurrency but does not make access to a shared mutable object exclusive.

questions.text: What does a semaphore's acquire() operation do to its count?
options: Always decrements it, even below zero
Increments it if the count is currently positive
Resets it to the value it was created with
Waits until the count is positive, then decrements it
questions.explanation: If the count is zero, acquire() blocks the caller. Once a slot is available, the count is decremented atomically and the caller proceeds; release() increments it again and may wake a waiter.

questions.text: A bug calls release() one extra time. What happens with threading.Semaphore(1) compared with threading.BoundedSemaphore(1)?
options: Both raise ValueError
Semaphore silently rises to 2; BoundedSemaphore raises ValueError
Semaphore raises RuntimeError; BoundedSemaphore ignores the call
Both silently rise to 2, letting two threads in at once
questions.explanation: A plain semaphore lets the count grow past its initial value, which can quietly admit too many threads. BoundedSemaphore checks for this and raises ValueError: Semaphore released too many times.

questions.text: Which statement describes a difference between a binary semaphore and a mutex?
options: A binary semaphore can count to any positive value
A binary semaphore must be released by the thread that acquired it
A binary semaphore can be acquired by one thread and released by another
A binary semaphore can hold negative values
questions.explanation: A mutex has an owner that must unlock it. A binary semaphore has no ownership, which makes it suitable for signalling between threads.

questions.text: Which two mechanisms are commonly combined to build a thread-safe blocking queue in C++?
options: A mutex and a condition variable
A semaphore and a thread-local variable
An atomic counter and a spinlock
Nothing, since std::queue is already thread-safe
questions.explanation: The mutex protects the queue's contents, and the condition variable lets consumers sleep until an item arrives. std::queue itself provides no thread safety.

questions.text: In Python, which ready-made class provides a thread-safe FIFO for producer-consumer code?
options: collections.OrderedDict
threading.local
threading.Barrier
queue.Queue
questions.explanation: queue.Queue handles its own locking, and get() can block until an item is available. With maxsize, put() also blocks when it is full, giving backpressure.

questions.text: What is a monitor in concurrent programming?
options: A construct that combines shared state, a mutex and condition variables
A debugging tool that records the activity of every thread
A background thread that watches other threads for crashes
An OS service that reports how much CPU each thread uses
questions.explanation: A monitor lets only one thread at a time run inside it and provides condition variables for waiting on state changes. A bounded buffer with not_full and not_empty conditions is a classic example.

questions.text: What does executor.submit(fn, x) return for a concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor?
options: The value of fn(x), after waiting for it
The Thread object that will run fn
A Future representing the pending call
None, because results are discarded
questions.explanation: submit() schedules the call on a worker thread and returns immediately. Call future.result() to wait for the value or re-raise the exception from fn.

questions.text: Why are thread pools useful?
options: Threads in a pool can share data more easily than other threads
They automatically prevent data races between tasks
They guarantee that tasks run in the order they were submitted
They reuse threads, avoiding the cost of creating a thread for every task
questions.explanation: A pool keeps a bounded set of worker threads that pull tasks from a queue. This amortises creation cost and limits how many threads run at once.

questions.text: A server starts a new thread for every incoming request, with no limit. What is the main risk during a burst of 10,000 requests?
options: Thousands of threads exhaust memory and drown the CPU in scheduling overhead
The OS merges the extra threads into one, serializing the requests
Requests are processed strictly in arrival order, so latency doubles
New threads cannot be created while another thread holds a lock
questions.explanation: On-demand threads cost creation time, stack memory and context switches. A bounded pool with a queue caps the thread count and applies backpressure instead.

questions.text: What does threading.Timer(5.0, f).start() do?
options: Calls f once, in a new thread, after about 5 seconds
Calls f every 5 seconds until the timer is cancelled
Blocks the calling thread for 5 seconds and then calls f
Runs f and raises an error if it takes longer than 5 seconds
questions.explanation: A Timer is a thread that waits and then runs its function once. cancel() stops it if called before the delay ends; periodic work needs a loop.

questions.text: What does Thread.is_alive() return?
options: The thread's numeric identifier, or None
The thread's exit code, once it has finished
Whether the thread was created as a daemon
Whether it has started and not yet finished
questions.explanation: is_alive() is True from just before run() starts until just after it returns. It is often used after a join() with a timeout to see whether the thread finished.

questions.text: Which threading object lets one thread set a flag that releases every thread blocked in its wait() and stays set for later callers?
options: threading.Lock
threading.Event
threading.Barrier
threading.Timer
questions.explanation: Event.set() wakes all waiters, and later wait() calls return immediately until clear() is called. A barrier releases threads only once enough of them arrive.

questions.text: What is the difference between calling t.start() and calling t.run() on a threading.Thread?
options: They are equivalent, because start() is simply an alias for run()
start() runs the target in a new thread; run() runs it in the calling thread
run() creates the OS thread; start() only schedules it to run
start() waits for the target to finish; run() returns immediately
questions.explanation: start() creates the OS thread, which then calls run(). Calling run() directly is just an ordinary function call, so nothing runs concurrently.

questions.text: What is the recommended way to stop a long-running Python worker thread?
options: Call thread.stop() and then join() it
Call thread.terminate() to end it at once
Call thread.kill(signal.SIGTERM) on it
Signal it with an Event it checks, then join() it
questions.explanation: Python threads have no stop, terminate or kill method. Cooperative stopping lets the worker finish its current step and clean up before it exits.

questions.text: What happens if you call start() twice on the same threading.Thread object?
options: The thread restarts from the beginning
A RuntimeError is raised
The second call is silently ignored
The second call blocks until the first run completes
questions.explanation: A thread object can be started only once (RuntimeError: threads can only be started once). To run the work again, create a new Thread.

questions.text: What is a spinlock, and when is it appropriate?
options: A lock that keeps a thread asleep until the OS wakes it, for long waits
A lock that busy-waits until it is free, for very short critical sections on multicore machines
A lock that rotates ownership between threads in a fixed order, for fairness
A lock used only to protect disk I/O, for slow storage devices
questions.explanation: Spinning avoids the cost of sleeping and waking when the holder, running on another core, will release the lock almost immediately. For longer waits it wastes CPU time that other threads could use.

questions.text: What is a livelock?
options: A thread that is permanently blocked waiting on one lock
Another name for a deadlock between two threads
A lock that keeps a thread alive after the program exits
Threads that keep reacting to each other but make no progress
questions.explanation: Livelocked threads are active, for example repeatedly backing off and retrying in step, but no work gets done. In a deadlock the threads are blocked instead.

questions.text: What is thread-local storage, such as Python's threading.local()?
options: Memory that only the main thread may access
Data for which each thread sees its own independent copy
A cache located physically close to the CPU core
Encrypted storage for sensitive thread data
questions.explanation: Each thread that sets an attribute on a threading.local() object gets its own value, so no locking is needed for that data.

questions.text: What is the difference between a lock-free and a wait-free algorithm?
options: Lock-free guarantees some thread progresses; wait-free bounds every thread's steps
Lock-free uses no atomic instructions at all; wait-free uses atomics but no mutexes
Lock-free code works only on one core; wait-free code scales to many cores
Lock-free threads never wait for I/O; wait-free threads never sleep or block
questions.explanation: In a lock-free algorithm a stalled thread cannot block the others, but an individual thread may starve while others keep winning. Wait-free is stronger: no thread can starve.

questions.text: What does a compare-and-swap (CAS) operation do?
options: Swaps the values of two variables and returns the larger
Compares two memory regions and reports the first difference
Atomically writes a new value only if the old one is as expected
Exchanges the stacks of two threads during a context switch
questions.explanation: CAS reports whether it succeeded, so a thread can retry with a fresh value if another thread changed the location first. It is the building block of many lock-free algorithms.

questions.text: What is the thundering herd problem?
options: Too many threads being created at once when the program starts
Threads that each keep spawning more and more child threads
Memory exhaustion caused by large thread stacks
Many waiting threads being woken at once when only one can proceed
questions.explanation: After a broadcast wakeup, all the threads compete for the resource and most go back to sleep, wasting CPU time and causing contention. Waking only one waiter avoids it.

questions.text:
What problem does this C++ code have when several threads run it on a shared std::atomic<int> counter?

counter.store(counter.load() + 1);
options: Updates can be lost, because another thread can change counter between the load and the store
None, because both calls are atomic
It is undefined behavior, because atomics cannot be loaded and stored in one statement
It deadlocks, because load() locks the atomic until store() is called
questions.explanation: Each call is atomic, so there is no data race, but the read-modify-write sequence is not. counter.fetch_add(1) performs the whole increment as one atomic operation.

questions.text: Ten threads each run counter.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed) 100,000 times on a std::atomic<int>. After joining them all, what does main print?
options: A value that varies, because relaxed operations can lose increments
Exactly 1000000
At most 100000, because relaxed increments from different threads overwrite each other
Nothing is guaranteed, because relaxed atomics are a data race
questions.explanation: Every read-modify-write on one atomic is indivisible whatever the ordering, so no increment is lost, and join() makes the final value visible. Relaxed only means the counter does not order other memory.

questions.text: Is std::atomic<T> guaranteed to be lock-free for every type T?
options: Yes, the standard requires a hardware instruction for every atomic type
Yes, but only for types smaller than a cache line
No; check std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free or is_lock_free()
No; only std::atomic<bool> is ever lock-free
questions.explanation: The standard guarantees lock-freedom for std::atomic_flag, not for std::atomic<T> in general; large types may use an internal lock. int-sized atomics are lock-free on mainstream platforms.

questions.text: A producer fills a buffer and then stores ready = true with memory_order_release. Which operation must the consumer perform on ready so it is guaranteed to see the buffer's contents?
options: A load with memory_order_relaxed that reads true
A plain non-atomic read of ready in a loop
A store with memory_order_acquire to ready
A load with memory_order_acquire that reads true
questions.explanation: A release store paired with an acquire load that reads its value makes all writes before the store visible after the load. Relaxed orders only the flag itself, and an acquire store is not valid.

questions.text:
Both atomic operations below use memory_order_relaxed. Which statement about the program is correct?

int data = 0;
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};

void producer() {
    data = 42;
    ready.store(true, std::memory_order_relaxed);
}

void consumer() {
    while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {}
    std::cout << data << '\n';
}
options: It always prints 42, because the consumer waits until ready is true
It may print 0, but otherwise the program is well defined
The accesses to data are a data race, so the behavior is undefined
It never terminates, because relaxed stores never become visible
questions.explanation: Relaxed operations create no happens-before edge, so the write and read of data are unsynchronized; ThreadSanitizer reports a race. Using release for the store and acquire for the load fixes it.

questions.text:
Two threads run these functions concurrently. Which change prevents the possible deadlock?

def task1():
    with lock1:
        with lock2:
            work()

def task2():
    with lock2:
        with lock1:
            work()
options: Add time.sleep() between the two with statements
Replace both locks with threading.Event objects
Make both functions acquire lock1 before lock2
Start task2 before task1
questions.explanation: Opposite acquisition orders can form a cycle where each thread holds one lock and waits for the other. A single global lock order breaks the circular wait.

questions.text: Two C++ functions need mutexes a and b, and different call sites lock them in different orders. Which C++17 construct avoids deadlock without agreeing on an order?
options: Two nested std::lock_guard objects, one per mutex
a.try_lock() followed by b.lock()
std::scoped_lock lk(a, b);
std::unique_lock lk(a, std::defer_lock); with no further calls
questions.explanation: std::scoped_lock with several mutexes uses the same deadlock-avoidance algorithm as std::lock and releases them all at scope exit. Nested guards still depend on lock order.

questions.text: In C++, what is the consequence of a data race on a plain (non-atomic) int?
options: The final value is always one of the values that were written
The program throws std::system_error when the race occurs
The behavior of the whole program is undefined
The compiler rejects the program at compile time
questions.explanation: The C++ memory model makes data races undefined behavior, so even a seemingly correct result proves nothing. Use a mutex or std::atomic for shared data; -fsanitize=thread helps find races.

questions.text: In C++, thread A updates balance while holding mutex_m. Thread B reads balance without locking anything. Is B's read safe?
options: No, every conflicting access to balance must use the same mutex
Yes, because only writes need to hold the mutex
Yes, because thread A holds the mutex during its write
No, because reads are never allowed while a mutex exists
questions.explanation: A lock protects only the code that uses it. B's unsynchronized read races with A's write, which is undefined behavior in C++; B must lock mutex_m too.

questions.text: A CPU-bound C++ program runs well with 8 threads on an 8-core machine. What usually happens if it uses 200 threads instead?
options: It becomes about 25 times faster, one thread per unit of work
It runs at the same speed, since extra threads simply wait
It fails, because the OS allows only one thread per CPU core
It gains nothing and may slow down from context switching and contention
questions.explanation: Once every core is busy, extra CPU-bound threads only add scheduling overhead, cache thrashing and contention. More threads do not mean more performance.

questions.text: Why prefer std::lock_guard or std::scoped_lock over calling lock() and unlock() by hand?
options: They make the mutex faster to acquire under contention
They allow several threads to own the mutex at the same time
They unlock automatically on scope exit, even on exceptions
They turn the mutex into a recursive mutex automatically
questions.explanation: RAII guards unlock in their destructor, so an early return or exception cannot leave the mutex locked.

questions.text: In Node.js, the main thread passes an ArrayBuffer to a Worker in transferList. What does buf.byteLength report in the main thread afterwards?
options: 0, because the buffer was detached when ownership moved to the worker
The original size, because transferred buffers are shared like SharedArrayBuffer
The original size, because the worker received a structured-clone copy
It throws, because a transferred buffer cannot be inspected
questions.explanation: Transfer moves ownership without copying, leaving the sender's buffer detached. A SharedArrayBuffer instead stays usable on both sides and needs Atomics for coordinated access.

questions.text: In a producer-consumer architecture, how should the average consumption rate relate to the average production rate?
options: The consumption rate should be lower than the production rate
The consumption rate should be greater than or equal to the production rate
The two rates must be exactly equal at every single moment
The rates do not matter as long as the buffer is large enough
questions.explanation: If consumers are slower on average, the buffer grows without bound or producers stall forever. Short bursts are absorbed by the buffer, but long-run consumption must keep up.

questions.text: Which architecture consists of a chain of producer-consumer pairs?
options: Pipeline
Client-server
Peer-to-peer
Master-worker
questions.explanation: In a pipeline each stage consumes the previous stage's output and produces input for the next, such as download, then parse, then write.

questions.text: What is a key advantage of using processes instead of threads?
options: Processes share all their memory with each other by default
Processes are cheaper to create and switch between
Processes never need any synchronization for shared files
A crash or stray write in one process cannot corrupt another's private memory
questions.explanation: Each process normally has its own address space, so a stray write or crash stays contained. The cost is higher start-up overhead and explicit IPC for sharing data.

questions.text: In Python's multiprocessing, how do the fork and spawn start methods differ?
options: fork copies the parent process; spawn starts a fresh Python interpreter
fork is available only on Windows, and spawn only on Linux
fork creates a thread in the parent; spawn creates a process
fork shares the parent's memory for writes; spawn copies it
questions.explanation: A forked child inherits a snapshot of the parent's memory. A spawned child starts a new interpreter and receives its target and arguments by pickling, so start-up is slower.

questions.text: Starting with Python 3.14, which start method does multiprocessing use by default on Linux?
options: fork
spawn
forkserver
threads
questions.explanation: Python 3.14 stopped defaulting to fork everywhere. Windows and macOS use spawn, and other POSIX platforms such as Linux use forkserver; Python 3.13 and earlier used fork on Linux.

questions.text: A script calls mp.Process(target=f).start() at module level, with no if __name__ == "__main__": guard. It works on Python 3.12 on Linux but fails with RuntimeError on Python 3.14. Why?
options: Python 3.14 forbids creating processes outside a function
Python 3.14 requires every target function to be declared async
The 3.14 default, forkserver, makes the child import the main module, re-running the start-up code
The 3.12 child was a thread, while the 3.14 child is a real process
questions.explanation: With spawn or forkserver the child imports the main module as __mp_main__, so unguarded code tries to start a process during bootstrapping and Python raises RuntimeError. fork copies the parent instead, which hid the bug.

questions.text:
A script sets CONFIG["mode"] = "changed" inside if __name__ == "__main__": and then starts a multiprocessing.Process whose target prints CONFIG["mode"]. What does the child print with the default start method on Linux?

CONFIG = {"mode": "default"}

def show():
    print(CONFIG["mode"])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    CONFIG["mode"] = "changed"
    p = multiprocessing.Process(target=show)
    p.start()
    p.join()
options: changed on every Python version
default on every Python version
changed on Python 3.12 (fork), but default on Python 3.14 (forkserver)
default on Python 3.12, but changed on Python 3.14
questions.explanation: A forked child copies the parent's current memory. A spawn or forkserver child re-imports the module, which re-runs CONFIG = {...} but not the guarded block; pass needed state as arguments instead.

questions.text: A Python 3.12 program on Linux passes a lambda as the target of a multiprocessing.Process. What happens?
options: It fails with every start method, because a target must be a named function
It works with every start method, because the target runs in the parent
It works with spawn but fails with fork
It works with fork, but spawn and forkserver raise a pickling error
questions.explanation: A forked child already has the function in its copied memory. spawn and forkserver must pickle the target, and a lambda cannot be pickled by reference, so define workers at module level.

questions.text: A Python 3.12 program starts a background thread and then creates a multiprocessing.Process with the default fork method on Linux. Why does Python emit a DeprecationWarning?
options: The child process inherits every thread, so the work is done twice
Only the forking thread is copied, so a lock held by another thread can stay locked in the child
fork() cannot be called while any thread is running and fails
Threads and processes cannot exist in the same Python program
questions.explanation: After fork() the child has a single thread, and locks other threads held at that moment are never released, so the child can deadlock. That risk is one reason Python 3.14 stopped using fork by default.

questions.text: When is shared memory preferable to message passing between processes?
options: When the processes run on different machines in a cluster
When same-host processes swap large data with low latency
When you want to avoid any need for synchronization
When messages must survive a crash of either process
questions.explanation: Shared memory avoids copying data through an IPC channel. It only works on one machine and requires explicit synchronization of the shared region.

questions.text: What is a multiprocessing.Queue used for?
options: Ordering processes by priority for the scheduler
Limiting how many processes can exist
Storing the PIDs of child processes
Passing picklable objects safely between processes
questions.explanation: The queue serializes objects and handles the underlying pipe and locking, so processes can exchange messages without sharing ordinary Python objects.

questions.text: A child process puts a 10 MB object on a multiprocessing.Queue. The parent calls p.join() before q.get(). What happens?
options: The join can hang, because the child waits for its queued data to be consumed before exiting
The join returns at once, because put() copied the data into the parent
The data is dropped when the child exits, so q.get() blocks forever
Python raises RuntimeError, because joining before reading is forbidden
questions.explanation: A child that has put items on a queue does not terminate until its feeder thread has flushed them into the pipe. Get the results first, then join.

questions.text: Which multiprocessing classes store simple numeric data in shared memory that several processes can update?
options: Queue and Pipe
Pool and Process
Value and Array
Event and Barrier
questions.explanation: Value('i', 0) and Array('d', 10) live in shared memory, so all processes see the same data. Queues and pipes copy messages instead.

questions.text:
Why does this worker wrap the update in get_lock()?

def increment(shared_value):
    with shared_value.get_lock():
        shared_value.value += 1
options: Value objects cannot be read at all without holding a lock
The lock copies the current value into the child process
It is required to keep the process from becoming a zombie
+= is a read-modify-write, so concurrent updates could be lost
questions.explanation: The read, add and write steps can interleave across processes; four processes doing 50,000 unlocked increments each can end far below 200,000. get_lock() returns the lock that protects the value, making each update exclusive.

questions.text: What does multiprocessing.Pool provide?
options: A set of reusable worker processes that run tasks in parallel
A pool of shared variables that processes can lock
A memory pool that reduces allocation overhead for processes
A registry of every process currently running on the system
questions.explanation: A pool starts its workers once and distributes many tasks to them, which avoids the cost of creating a process per task.

questions.text: In Python's multiprocessing.Pool, how does map() differ from apply_async()?
options: map() blocks for all results; apply_async() returns at once
map() runs one call; apply_async() runs a list of calls
map() uses threads; apply_async() uses processes
map() is deprecated; apply_async() replaces it
questions.explanation: map() applies a function to every item and returns the result list once all are done. apply_async() schedules one call and lets you collect its result later with .get().

questions.text: A function submitted with pool.apply_async(f) raises ValueError. When does the parent process see the error?
options: Never, because exceptions in workers are silently discarded
Immediately, because the whole pool shuts down with it
Only in the worker's log output, as a printed traceback
When it calls .get(), which re-raises the ValueError
questions.explanation: The pool pickles the exception and sends it back with the result. .get() re-raises it in the parent, so errors are handled where the result is used.

questions.text: A multiprocessing.Process target raises ValueError. What happens when the parent calls p.join()?
options: join() re-raises the ValueError in the parent
join() returns normally, and p.exitcode is 1
join() blocks forever because the child crashed
The parent process is terminated as well
questions.explanation: A plain Process does not send exceptions back to the parent; the child just prints a traceback. Check exitcode after join(), or report errors through a queue or use a pool or executor.

questions.text: What is a zombie process?
options: A finished child whose exit status has not been collected
A process that is still running but no longer responds
A process that keeps consuming memory after it is killed
A process that ignores every signal, including SIGTERM
questions.explanation: A zombie no longer runs, but its process-table entry remains until the parent reads its exit status. Many zombies can exhaust PIDs or process-table capacity.

questions.text: A C parent forks a child that returns immediately, then sleeps without calling wait(). What does ps -o stat=,cmd= -p <child-pid> show on Linux during that sleep?
options: Nothing, because the child's entry was removed when it exited
S (sleeping), because the child is waiting for its parent
Z and <defunct>, because the child is a zombie
T (stopped), because the child is waiting to be reaped
questions.explanation: The exited child keeps its process-table entry until the parent reaps it, and ps marks it Z with <defunct>. Calling wait() or waitpid() removes it.

questions.text: How does a parent process prevent its finished children from remaining zombies?
options: By sending each child SIGKILL after it exits
By closing its standard output before forking
By lowering each child's priority with nice
By calling wait() or waitpid() for each child
questions.explanation: Waiting reaps the child and removes its process-table entry. In Python, Process.join() does this for you.

questions.text:
What does this C program print after reaping its child?

int main(void) {
    pid_t p = fork();
    if (p == 0)
        exit(3);
    int status;
    waitpid(p, &status, 0);
    printf("%d %d\n", WIFEXITED(status), WEXITSTATUS(status));
}
options: 1 3
0 3
3 0
1 0
questions.explanation: waitpid() stores an encoded status. WIFEXITED is true because the child exited normally, and WEXITSTATUS extracts the exit code 3.

questions.text: On a UNIX-like system, what happens to a running child process when its parent terminates?
options: It keeps running and is reparented to PID 1 or a subreaper
The kernel terminates the child along with its parent
The child becomes a zombie until the system reboots
The child is paused until a new parent claims it
questions.explanation: The orphan continues normally. Its new parent collects its exit status when it finishes, so it does not stay a zombie.

questions.text: In Python's multiprocessing, how does Process.terminate() differ from Process.kill() on POSIX systems?
options: terminate() pauses the process; kill() stops it
terminate() sends SIGTERM; kill() sends SIGKILL
terminate() is for daemons; kill() is for all processes
They are identical aliases for the same method
questions.explanation: With Python's default handling, both end the child without running finally blocks, and exitcode becomes -15 or -9. A process can install a SIGTERM handler, but SIGKILL cannot be caught.

questions.text: A process reads from a pipe until EOF, but it never sees EOF even after the writer finishes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The pipe's buffer is too small for all the data written
Pipes never report EOF, so the reader must count the bytes itself
The writer used print() instead of os.write()
A copy of the write end is still open somewhere, maybe in the reader
questions.explanation: A reader sees EOF only after every write endpoint is closed. Inherited, unused pipe ends must be closed in both parent and child.

questions.text: A process writes two 100-byte messages to a pipe. What can the reader's first read(4096) return?
options: Exactly the first 100-byte message, every single time
Nothing at all until the writer closes its end of the pipe
Any amount, such as part of a message or both messages joined together
The second message, because pipes are last-in, first-out
questions.explanation: A pipe carries a byte stream with no message boundaries. Use fixed-size records, a length prefix or a delimiter to split it back into messages.

questions.text: What is a named pipe (FIFO) on a POSIX system?
options: A pipe whose data is labelled with a message name by the sender
A pipe with a filesystem name that unrelated processes can open
A faster pipe that bypasses the kernel's buffers
A pipe that can only carry newline-terminated text
questions.explanation: An anonymous pipe is shared only through inheritance, usually between parent and child. A FIFO has a path, so any process with permission can open it.

questions.text: What does setting daemon=True on a multiprocessing.Process do?
options: Runs the process with elevated, administrator-level privileges
Makes the process immune to signals such as SIGTERM
Makes the parent terminate the child when the parent exits normally
Lets the process share memory with other daemons
questions.explanation: Python's exit handling terminates daemonic children instead of waiting for them; if the parent is killed by SIGKILL, the child keeps running as an orphan. A daemonic process may not create child processes.

questions.text: On an 8-core machine, which approach best speeds up CPU-bound pure-Python work in CPython 3.12?
options: A ThreadPoolExecutor with 8 worker threads
An asyncio event loop running 8 tasks
A single thread with a higher OS priority
A ProcessPoolExecutor with 8 worker processes
questions.explanation: Each process has its own interpreter and GIL, so CPU-bound Python code can run in parallel across cores. Threads and asyncio in the default GIL build take turns on one GIL.

questions.text: What is copy-on-write in the context of fork()?
options: The child receives a full copy of the parent's memory before it starts
Parent and child share memory pages until one of them writes to a page
Writes in the child are copied back into the parent
Files are copied when a forked process writes to them
questions.explanation: Copying is deferred until a write occurs, which makes fork() fast. Logically the memories are still separate: a write is never seen by the other process.

questions.text: What does a multiprocessing.Manager provide?
options: Control over process priorities and CPU affinity
Automatic restart of worker processes that crash
A way to allocate raw shared memory pages directly
A server process that holds shared objects behind proxies
questions.explanation: Manager proxies let several processes modify shared dicts, lists and other objects. Every access goes through the manager process, which is slower than Value or Array.

questions.text: What happens to open file descriptors when a process calls fork()?
options: They are closed automatically in the child
The child inherits copies referring to the same open files
They become invalid in both processes until reopened
The child receives read-only versions of them
questions.explanation: Inherited descriptors share the same underlying open files, including file offsets. That is why unused pipe ends must be closed in each process.

questions.text: What does os.fork() return?
options: The child's PID in both processes
0 in the parent and the parent's PID in the child
0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent
True if the fork succeeded, otherwise False
questions.explanation: Both processes continue from the same call, so the return value tells them apart. A negative value is never returned in Python; failures raise OSError.

questions.text:
How many lines does this C program print?

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        fork();
    printf("x\n");
    while (wait(NULL) > 0) {}
}
questions.explanation: Every existing process forks in each iteration, doubling the count: $2^3 = 8$ processes reach the printf.

questions.text:
This program's output is redirected to a file with ./a.out > out.txt. What does out.txt contain?

int main(void) {
    printf("hello\n");
    fork();
    while (wait(NULL) > 0) {}
}
options: hello twice, because the unflushed buffer is copied into the child
hello once, because the printf runs before fork()
Nothing, because the child closes the shared file
hello once, followed by an error from the child
questions.explanation: Output to a file is fully buffered, so hello is still in the stdio buffer at fork() and both processes flush it at exit. On a terminal stdout is line-buffered and it prints once; call fflush(stdout) before forking.

questions.text:
What does this C program print, assuming echo is on the PATH?

int main(void) {
    printf("before\n");
    fflush(stdout);
    execlp("echo", "echo", "replaced", (char *)NULL);
    printf("after\n");
    return 1;
}
options: before, replaced, then after
before, then after
before, then replaced
replaced only
questions.explanation: A successful exec replaces the process image, keeping the PID, so the code after it never runs. Only if execlp fails does it return and print after.

questions.text:
What value of x does the parent in this C program print?

int x = 1;

int main(void) {
    pid_t p = fork();
    if (p == 0) {
        x = 42;
        return 0;
    }
    waitpid(p, NULL, 0);
    printf("%d\n", x);
}
options: 1
42, because forked processes share global variables
42 or 1, depending on which process runs first
0, because fork() resets globals in the parent
questions.explanation: After fork() parent and child have logically separate memory, so the child's write is never seen by the parent. Use IPC or explicitly shared memory such as mmap(MAP_SHARED) to pass changes.

questions.text: What is process (CPU) affinity?
options: A measure of how well two processes cooperate
Restricting a process to run on a chosen set of CPU cores
The amount of memory shared between processes
The parent-child relationship between processes
questions.explanation: Pinning a process to cores, for example with taskset -c 0-7, can improve cache and NUMA locality and reduce migration. The scheduler then only places it on the allowed cores.

questions.text: How does a signal differ from a message in IPC?
options: Signals carry more data than messages do
Messages can only be exchanged between threads
A signal is a bare notification; a message carries data
Signals need a shared memory region to work
questions.explanation: A signal such as SIGTERM tells a process that an event occurred but carries little information. Messages through queues, pipes or sockets transfer actual data.

questions.text: A pool of 8 database connections is shared by many worker processes. Which primitive bounds the number of workers using a connection at once?
options: A mutex
A barrier for 8 parties
A condition variable with no predicate
A counting semaphore initialised to 8
questions.explanation: Each worker acquires the semaphore before taking a connection and releases it afterwards. When all 8 slots are in use, further workers wait.

questions.text: A bounded buffer with N slots is implemented with semaphores empty, full and a mutex m. What are their initial values?
options: empty = N, full = 0, m = 1
empty = 0, full = N, m = 1
empty = N, full = N, m = 0
empty = 1, full = 1, m = N
questions.explanation: Initially every slot is free and no item is available. Producers wait on empty, consumers wait on full, and the binary semaphore m starts unlocked.

questions.text: Every process acquires resources in the same global order: DB, then Cache, then Log. Which deadlock condition does this break?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
questions.explanation: If everyone requests resources in the same order, no process can hold a later resource while waiting for an earlier one, so a waiting cycle cannot form.

questions.text: In a simple readers-preference reader-writer lock, what is the main risk?
options: Readers can corrupt the data by reading concurrently
Writers can starve if new readers keep arriving
Two writers can write at the same time
Readers deadlock whenever a writer is waiting
questions.explanation: The lock lets new readers join while any reader is active, so a waiting writer may never get exclusive access. Writer-preference or fair locks address this.

questions.text: What is a memory-mapped file, and how can it be used for IPC?
options: A file mapped into memory, which several processes can share
A file kept only in RAM and never written to disk
A compressed copy of a process's memory saved to disk
A log of every memory access that a process makes
questions.explanation: With mmap and MAP_SHARED, processes that map the same file see the same pages. Like other shared memory, access still needs synchronization.

questions.text: Two worker processes split 10 tasks statically: the first five go to A and the last five to B. Every task takes 50 ms except the last, which takes 500 ms. When are both done?
options: After about 475 ms, half of the total work
After about 500 ms, the length of the longest task
After about 700 ms, when worker B finishes
After about 950 ms, the sum of all the tasks
questions.explanation: Worker A needs $5 \times 50 = 250$ ms, but B needs $4 \times 50 + 500 = 700$ ms. Dynamic scheduling from a shared queue can cut this to about 500 ms if the long task starts early.

questions.text: In a work-stealing scheduler, where does an idle worker take tasks from?
options: From a single global queue shared by all workers
From the same end of a busy worker's deque that the owner uses
From the opposite end of a busy worker's deque to the one the owner uses
From whichever worker has the shortest queue, after checking them all
questions.explanation: The owner pushes and pops at one end (LIFO, good for cache locality), while thieves steal from the other end. Operations are mostly local, so contention stays low.

questions.text: In "power of two choices" load balancing, where does a new task go?
options: To the worker with the shortest queue among all workers
To the less loaded of two randomly sampled workers
To two workers, keeping whichever result arrives first
To workers in strict round-robin order
questions.explanation: Sampling just two workers is cheap yet greatly reduces the maximum queue length compared with purely random assignment.

questions.text: A program spends 20% of its run time in code that cannot be parallelised. By Amdahl's law, what speedup can it reach on 8 processors?
options: $8\times$
$6.4\times$
$5\times$
$3.33\times$
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{0.2 + 0.8/8} = \frac{1}{0.3} \approx 3.33$. Even with unlimited processors the speedup cannot exceed $1/0.2 = 5$, because the sequential part never shrinks.

questions.text: Two processes repeatedly increment different int fields of one struct in shared memory, and the program scales badly. What is a likely cause and fix?
options: The fields race with each other, so each needs its own mutex
False sharing of one cache line; align each field to its own cache line
Shared memory is uncached, so copy the struct into a pipe instead
The kernel serializes all writes to shared pages, so use threads
questions.explanation: Adjacent fields often share a 64-byte cache line, which bounces between cores on every write although the data is independent. Padding or alignas(64) gives each field its own line.

questions.text: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
options: Vertical adds CPU or RAM to one machine; horizontal adds more machines
Vertical adds more machines; horizontal adds CPU or RAM to one machine
Vertical scales storage; horizontal scales network bandwidth
Vertical uses threads; horizontal uses processes
questions.explanation: Scaling up is simpler but limited by the largest available machine. Scaling out, for example behind a load balancer, goes further but adds distribution and failure handling.

questions.text: What is the main difference in isolation between containers and virtual machines?
options: Containers each run their own kernel; VMs share the host kernel
Containers share the host kernel; each VM runs its own guest OS kernel
Containers cannot run more than one process; VMs can run many
Containers isolate nothing; VMs isolate only the filesystem
questions.explanation: Containers isolate processes with kernel features such as namespaces, so they start quickly and stay light. A VM boots a full guest OS on a hypervisor, which costs more but isolates more strongly.

questions.text: What does Node.js's child_process.fork() do?
