options: It calls the POSIX fork() system call to duplicate the Node.js process
It creates a worker thread that shares the parent's heap
It starts a new Node.js process running a module, with an IPC channel for send() and 'message'
It runs a shell command and buffers its whole output
questions.explanation: Despite the name, Node's fork() spawns a fresh Node.js process rather than duplicating the current one. exec() is the helper that runs a shell command and buffers its output.

questions.text:
Roughly how long does this C++ program take, and why?

using namespace std::chrono_literals;

int main() {
    std::async(std::launch::async, [] { std::this_thread::sleep_for(500ms); });
    std::async(std::launch::async, [] { std::this_thread::sleep_for(500ms); });
}
options: About 0 ms, because both tasks run in the background after main returns
About 500 ms, because the two tasks run in parallel
About 1000 ms, because each discarded future blocks in its destructor
It does not compile, because the futures are not stored
questions.explanation: A future returned by std::async waits for its task when destroyed, so each temporary blocks until its task ends. Storing both futures and then calling get() overlaps them; compilers warn about the discarded [[nodiscard]] result.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a future?
options: It is a placeholder for a result that may not have been computed yet
It schedules a task to run later on a thread pool
It records how a program should behave on its next run
It retries an operation automatically whenever it fails
questions.explanation: A future starts pending and later completes with a value or an error. The work itself is done elsewhere, for example by a thread or an event loop.

questions.text: A function launched with std::async throws an exception. What happens when the caller calls get() on the returned future?
options: get() returns a default-constructed value
The program calls std::terminate immediately
The exception is re-thrown in the calling thread
get() blocks forever because no value was set
questions.explanation: The future stores the exception in its shared state, and get() re-throws it, so the caller can handle it with an ordinary try/catch.

questions.text: After int v = f.get(); returns on a std::future<int> f, what does f.valid() return?
options: true, so get() can be called again for the same value
true, but a second get() returns a default value
It throws, because valid() may not be called after get()
false, because get() released the shared state
questions.explanation: A std::future delivers its result once. Calling get() again on an invalid future is undefined behavior (libstdc++ throws std::future_error); use std::shared_future when the result must be read repeatedly.

questions.text: Several C++ threads all need to read the result of one asynchronous computation. What should they use?
options: A std::shared_future, for example from future.share()
One std::future, calling get() from every thread
A separate std::promise per thread, all set from the same future
A std::mutex that stores the result
questions.explanation: A std::future can be retrieved with get() only once. A std::shared_future can be copied, and every copy may call get() on the same result.

questions.text: What role does a std::promise play?
options: It launches a callable on a new thread and returns its result
It cancels a pending future and releases its shared state
It blocks until a given future becomes ready
It lets a producer set the value its future will deliver
questions.explanation: The producer calls set_value() or set_exception() on the promise. The consumer receives the result through the std::future obtained from get_future().

questions.text: When does a function launched with std::async(std::launch::deferred, f) run?
options: Immediately, on a newly created thread
Lazily, in the thread that first calls get() or wait()
Only when the future is destroyed at program exit
Later, on a worker thread from a global thread pool
questions.explanation: Deferred launch creates no thread; the call happens on demand in the waiting thread, and wait_for() reports std::future_status::deferred. Use std::launch::async to require asynchronous execution.

questions.text: How do you chain a second step after a std::future in standard C++20?
options: Call future.then(next_step)
Pass the future to std::async with std::launch::chain
Call get() and pass the result to the next step yourself
Assign next_step to future.on_ready
questions.explanation: std::future has no .then() in standard C++; that API stayed in a Technical Specification. Libraries such as Folly, HPX and Boost provide continuations as extensions.

questions.text: What do C++20 coroutines provide out of the box?
options: A built-in event loop that schedules every coroutine automatically
A standard thread pool on which co_await resumes coroutines
Asynchronous socket and file I/O in the standard library
Language support for suspending and resuming; a library supplies the task type and scheduler
questions.explanation: co_await, co_yield and co_return define suspension points, but the return type, promise type and scheduling come from code such as Boost.Asio or your own Task<T>.

questions.text: How does a coroutine differ from a regular function?
options: A coroutine always runs on its own dedicated thread
A coroutine cannot return a value to its caller
A coroutine always runs faster than a function
A coroutine can suspend and later resume where it left off
questions.explanation: A regular function runs until it returns. A coroutine can pause, for example at an await, letting a scheduler run other work before resuming it with its local state preserved.

questions.text: In Python, what happens when you call an async def function without awaiting it or turning it into a task?
options: Only a coroutine object is created; the body does not run
Its body runs synchronously and its result is discarded
Its body runs in a background thread automatically
A SyntaxError is raised at the call site
questions.explanation: Calling an async def function only creates a coroutine object. Its body runs when it is awaited or scheduled with asyncio.create_task(); otherwise RuntimeWarning: coroutine ... was never awaited appears when it is garbage-collected.

questions.text: How does calling a JavaScript async function differ from calling a Python async def function?
options: JavaScript runs the function on a worker thread; Python runs it on the event loop
JavaScript runs the body up to its first await; Python runs none of it yet
JavaScript returns the result directly; Python returns a future
There is no difference; both start running when awaited
questions.explanation: A JavaScript async function runs synchronously until its first await and returns a promise. A Python coroutine does nothing until it is awaited or scheduled.

questions.text: In Python, what does await x do inside a coroutine?
options: Starts a new operating-system thread to run the awaited call
Blocks the whole thread, and so every task, until it completes
Cancels the awaited operation if it is not already complete
Waits for x, yielding to the event loop if its result is not ready yet
questions.explanation: await waits for a result without blocking the thread. If the awaitable is not ready, control returns to the event loop, which resumes the coroutine later; if it completes immediately, no other task gets a turn.

questions.text:
In what order does this program record its steps?

import asyncio

log = []

async def quick():
    return 1

async def a():
    log.append("a1")
    await quick()
    log.append("a2")

async def b():
    log.append("b")

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(a(), b())
    print(log)

asyncio.run(main())
options: The order varies from run to run
questions.explanation: quick() returns without ever suspending, so await quick() does not yield to the event loop and a() runs to completion before b() starts. An await is only a potential switch point.

questions.text: What is an event loop?
options: A scheduler that resumes tasks and callbacks as I/O and timers complete
A loop that polls the keyboard and mouse for user input events
A debugging tool that traces the execution of asynchronous code
A thread pool that runs each coroutine on its own thread
questions.explanation: The event loop tracks pending I/O, timers and ready work. It can manage many concurrent operations on a single thread because tasks take turns as they become ready.

questions.text:
What does main print after scheduling a task?

import asyncio

async def main():
    out = []

    async def say():
        out.append("task")

    t = asyncio.create_task(say())
    out.append("after create_task")
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    out.append("after sleep")
    print(out)

asyncio.run(main())
options: ['task', 'after create_task', 'after sleep']
['after create_task', 'after sleep', 'task']
['after create_task', 'task', 'after sleep']
The order varies from run to run
questions.explanation: create_task() only schedules the coroutine; it starts when main yields to the loop at await asyncio.sleep(0). The single-threaded loop makes this order deterministic.

questions.text: How does asyncio.run(main()) differ from loop.run_until_complete(main())?
options: asyncio.run() creates, runs and closes a new loop; the other uses an existing loop
asyncio.run() runs the coroutine in a background thread; run_until_complete() uses the main thread
asyncio.run() returns immediately; run_until_complete() waits for the result
They are identical aliases kept for backward compatibility
questions.explanation: asyncio.run() is the high-level entry point that manages the loop's whole lifetime, including cleanup. run_until_complete() is a lower-level method on a loop you manage yourself.

questions.text: A coroutine already running under asyncio.run() calls asyncio.run(other()). What happens?
options: other() runs to completion on a second, nested event loop
other() is scheduled on the current loop and runs later
The current loop is closed and replaced by a new one
RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop
questions.explanation: asyncio.run() is meant to be the program's single entry point. Inside a coroutine, await other() or asyncio.create_task(other()) runs it on the existing loop instead.

questions.text:
What does this code print?

import asyncio

async def fetch(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(n / 10)
    return n

async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(fetch(3), fetch(1), fetch(2)))

asyncio.run(main())
options: [1, 2, 3]
[3, 1, 2]
[3, 2, 1]
The order varies from run to run
questions.explanation: The coroutines run concurrently and finish in the order 1, 2, 3, but gather() returns results in the order the awaitables were passed in.

questions.text:
What does this as_completed() loop print?

import asyncio

async def fetch(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(n / 10)
    return n

async def main():
    results = []
    for c in asyncio.as_completed([fetch(3), fetch(1), fetch(2)]):
        results.append(await c)
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
options: [1, 2, 3]
[3, 1, 2]
[3, 2, 1]
An error, because as_completed() accepts only tasks
questions.explanation: as_completed() yields awaitables in completion order, so the shortest sleep comes first. Use it to process each result as soon as it is ready, unlike the input-ordered list from gather().

questions.text: In await asyncio.gather(fail(), slow()), fail() raises ValueError while slow() is still sleeping. With the default arguments, what happens to slow()?
options: It is cancelled, and gather() raises an ExceptionGroup
It is cancelled, and gather() raises CancelledError
It keeps running, while gather() immediately raises the ValueError
gather() waits for it to finish and then raises the ValueError
questions.explanation: By default gather() propagates the first exception but does not cancel the other awaitables, which can be left running unobserved. asyncio.TaskGroup cancels the siblings instead.

questions.text: What does asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) change?
options: It cancels the remaining tasks as soon as one fails
Failed awaitables are retried automatically once
Exceptions are written to the log and then discarded
Exceptions appear in the result list instead of being raised
questions.explanation: Without it, the first exception is raised to the awaiting code. With it, every awaitable finishes and failures appear in their positions in the result list.

questions.text: One task inside an asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11+) raises ValueError. What happens to the other tasks in the group?
options: They keep running, and the error is raised once they finish
They are cancelled, then the error is raised in an ExceptionGroup
They are restarted from the beginning after a delay
They are paused until the failed task is retried
questions.explanation: A TaskGroup treats related tasks as one unit: a failure cancels the remaining tasks, waits for them to finish, then raises the collected errors, which except* ValueError can handle.

questions.text: How does asyncio.wait() differ from asyncio.gather()?
options: wait() cancels the pending tasks when it returns; gather() does not
wait() blocks the event loop thread; gather() does not
wait() always returns immediately; gather() waits for every task
wait() returns (done, pending) sets; gather() returns ordered results
questions.explanation: wait() can return when the first task completes or fails, via return_when, and leaves pending tasks running; you read results from the done tasks yourself. gather() waits for all and returns an ordered list.

questions.text: In Python 3.12, what happens when you call await asyncio.wait([fetch(1)]) with a bare coroutine object?
options: It wraps the coroutine in a task automatically, as in older versions
It raises TypeError, because wait() accepts only tasks and futures
It returns at once with the coroutine in the pending set
It runs the coroutine synchronously before waiting
questions.explanation: Passing coroutines to wait() was deprecated in 3.8 and is an error since 3.11. Create tasks first with asyncio.create_task(), or use gather(), which accepts coroutines.

questions.text:
Roughly how long does this program take to run?

import asyncio

async def work():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)

async def main():
    await work()
    await work()

asyncio.run(main())
options: About 0 seconds
About 1 second
About 2 seconds
About 4 seconds
questions.explanation: Each await waits for one work() to finish before starting the next, so the sleeps happen sequentially. asyncio.gather(work(), work()) would overlap them and take about 1 second.

questions.text:
Roughly how long does this gather() call take to finish?

import asyncio, time

async def work():
    time.sleep(1)

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(work(), work())

asyncio.run(main())
options: About 0 seconds
About 1 second
About 2 seconds
About 4 seconds
questions.explanation: time.sleep() blocks the event loop's only thread, so the two coroutines cannot overlap despite gather(). With await asyncio.sleep(1) the program would take about 1 second.

questions.text: How does await asyncio.sleep(1) differ from time.sleep(1) inside a coroutine?
options: They behave identically inside a coroutine
asyncio.sleep() runs on a separate thread; time.sleep() runs on the event loop
time.sleep() is asynchronous; asyncio.sleep() is not
asyncio.sleep() suspends one task; time.sleep() blocks the loop
questions.explanation: time.sleep() keeps the thread busy, so no other task can run during it. asyncio.sleep() hands control back to the loop until the timer expires.

questions.text: A coroutine must call a library function that performs blocking I/O. How can you keep the event loop responsive?
options: Wrap the library function in an async def
Offload it with await asyncio.to_thread(func)
Call it inside async with so it becomes nonblocking
Call asyncio.sleep(0) just before the blocking call
questions.explanation: Declaring a function async does not make its synchronous body nonblocking. Offloading it to a thread, with to_thread() or run_in_executor(), lets the loop keep running other tasks while the call waits.

questions.text: An asyncio server must run a CPU-heavy pure-Python function on CPython 3.12 without slowing other requests much. Which choice gives real parallelism?
options: await asyncio.to_thread(func), since threads run in parallel
Making func an async def and awaiting it
Calling func between two await asyncio.sleep(0) calls
await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, func) with a ProcessPoolExecutor
questions.explanation: A thread keeps the loop responsive, but in the GIL build it competes for the same GIL. Separate processes have their own interpreters, so the computation runs on another core.

questions.text: Where can the asyncio event loop switch from one running coroutine to another?
options: At any bytecode instruction, like OS thread preemption
Only when a coroutine returns or raises an exception
Only where the running coroutine suspends, such as at an await
Every 10 milliseconds, when a timer interrupt fires
questions.explanation: asyncio is cooperative. A coroutine that computes for a long time without awaiting keeps every other task waiting until it suspends or finishes.

questions.text: What is "callback hell", and how does async/await help?
options: Callbacks that run too fast to debug; await slows them down
Deeply nested callbacks; await lets the logic be written linearly
Callbacks that never execute; await forces them to run
Memory leaks caused by callbacks; await frees the memory
questions.explanation: Each dependent step used to be nested inside the previous step's callback. With await, sequential steps and try/except error handling read like ordinary synchronous code.

questions.text: In Node.js, Promise.all([fetch(a), fetch(b)]) rejects because the first request fails. What happens to the second request?
options: It keeps running; Promise.all only stops waiting for it
It is aborted automatically, closing its connection
It is retried until it succeeds
It is paused until the first request is retried
questions.explanation: Promise combinators observe promises but cannot stop the underlying work. To stop the other request, pass an AbortSignal to fetch() and abort it; use Promise.allSettled to collect every outcome.

questions.text: A producer coroutine calls await queue.put(item) on a full asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100). What happens?
options: The item is dropped silently to protect memory
queue.put() raises asyncio.QueueFull immediately
The queue grows beyond 100 items to make room
The producer waits until a consumer removes an item
questions.explanation: A bounded queue applies backpressure: fast producers are slowed to the consumers' pace instead of letting memory grow without limit. put_nowait() is the variant that raises QueueFull.

questions.text: What is async with used for?
options: Managing resources whose setup and cleanup must be awaited
Declaring variables that are shared between coroutines
Converting a synchronous block into asynchronous code
Running the body in parallel on several threads
questions.explanation: An async context manager awaits its __aenter__ and __aexit__ methods, so connections or files can be opened and closed without blocking the loop.

questions.text: What is async for used for?
options: Running each loop iteration on a separate thread
Iterating over a list of futures in completion order
Iterating where fetching each next item may need an await
Making an ordinary for loop run faster on the event loop
questions.explanation: async for calls __anext__() and awaits it for each item, so the loop can wait for data, such as rows from a stream, without blocking the event loop.

questions.text: What is an async generator in Python?
options: An async def function that contains yield
A tool that converts synchronous code into coroutines
A class that creates a new event loop for each value
A generator that runs on a background thread
questions.explanation: An async generator is consumed with async for and can await between yields, which makes it a convenient way to stream values that arrive over time.

questions.text: A coroutine sends requests to an API that allows at most 10 concurrent calls. Which asyncio primitive enforces the limit?
options: asyncio.Event, set after every 10 requests
asyncio.Lock, held for the whole batch
asyncio.Barrier(10) before each batch
asyncio.Semaphore(10) around each request
questions.explanation: Each request acquires the semaphore before calling the API. When 10 are in flight, further requests wait until one finishes and releases its slot.

questions.text:
What value of shared does this program print?

import asyncio

shared = 0

async def inc():
    global shared
    tmp = shared
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    shared = tmp + 1

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(*(inc() for _ in range(100)))
    print(shared)

asyncio.run(main())
options: 1
100
A value between 1 and 100 that varies from run to run
0
questions.explanation: Every task reads 0 before any of them resumes and writes, so all write 1. Even on one thread, an update that spans an await needs an asyncio.Lock.

questions.text: Single-threaded asyncio code updates shared state. When does it still need an asyncio.Lock?
options: Never, because only one coroutine runs at a time
Whenever two coroutines read the same variable
Only when the program uses more than one CPU core
When the update contains an await partway through
questions.explanation: Without an await inside the update, no other task can interleave. If the critical section suspends, another coroutine may see or change half-updated state.

questions.text: What is asyncio.Condition used for?
options: Waiting until shared state meets a condition, then being notified
Checking whether the event loop is currently running
Setting preconditions that a task must meet before it is created
Testing network conditions before sending requests
questions.explanation: It combines an asyncio.Lock with notification, mirroring threading.Condition. Coroutines await cond.wait_for(predicate) and producers call notify() after changing the state.

questions.text: An exception is raised inside a coroutine. Where does it surface?
options: Nowhere, because exceptions in coroutines are ignored
It always crashes the whole program immediately
In the code that awaits the coroutine or its task
Only in the event loop's debug log
questions.explanation: Awaiting re-raises the exception, so ordinary try/except works. If nobody awaits a failed task, the loop only logs Task exception was never retrieved and the program carries on.

questions.text: A coroutine calls asyncio.create_task(send_metrics()) and discards the returned task. What is the risk?
options: The task runs synchronously and blocks the caller until it finishes
The task is cancelled as soon as the calling coroutine returns
The loop keeps only a weak reference, so the task can be garbage-collected and its errors go unnoticed
The task runs twice, once for the call and once for the garbage collector
questions.explanation: The asyncio docs say to keep a reference to every task you create. Store it, for example in a set with a done callback, or use a TaskGroup so the task's lifetime and errors are owned.

questions.text: What happens when task.cancel() is called on a running asyncio task?
options: The task is stopped instantly, even in the middle of a statement
CancelledError is raised inside it at its current await
The task finishes normally but its result is discarded
The event loop is closed along with the task
questions.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative: the coroutine sees CancelledError at its current or next await. It should release resources in finally and normally let the error propagate.

questions.text: A task's coroutine catches asyncio.CancelledError, ignores it, and returns "done". After task.cancel(), what does await task give?
options: It raises CancelledError, because cancel() returned True
It raises InvalidStateError, because the task ignored cancellation
"done", and task.cancelled() is False
None, because a cancelled task has no result
questions.explanation: cancel() only requests cancellation by throwing CancelledError into the coroutine. Swallowing it defeats timeouts and TaskGroup cleanup, so re-raise it after cleaning up.

questions.text: In Python 3.11 and later, what exception does asyncio.wait_for() raise when the timeout expires?
options: The built-in TimeoutError
asyncio.CancelledError
concurrent.futures.CancelledError
asyncio.InvalidStateError
questions.explanation: Since 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError and concurrent.futures.TimeoutError are both aliases of the built-in TimeoutError. The awaited task is cancelled internally when the timeout expires.

questions.text: What does asyncio.timeout(5) (Python 3.11+) provide?
options: A global timeout applied to every coroutine in the program
A decorator that retries a coroutine for up to 5 seconds
A 5-second pause before the block starts running
An async context manager that cancels its block after 5 seconds
questions.explanation: async with asyncio.timeout(5): cancels the work inside if the deadline passes and converts that cancellation into TimeoutError when the block exits.

questions.text: What does await asyncio.shield(task) protect against?
options: Exceptions raised inside the shielded task
Outer cancellation propagating into the inner task
Timeouts raised by the task's own code
Other tasks reading or changing the task's state
questions.explanation: If the outer coroutine is cancelled, the shielded task keeps running, while the outer await still raises CancelledError.

questions.text: What does future.cancel() return for a concurrent.futures.Future whose call is already running?
options: False, because a running call cannot be cancelled
True, and the worker thread is stopped
None, after waiting for the call to finish
It raises CancelledError in the caller
questions.explanation: Only calls still waiting in the executor's queue can be cancelled. A running or finished call returns False, and its result can still be retrieved with result().

questions.text: How do you enable asyncio's debug mode to detect slow callbacks and never-awaited coroutines?
options: Call asyncio.debug() at start-up
Pass debug=True to asyncio.run()
Import the asyncio.debugger module
Pass --asyncio-debug to python
questions.explanation: There is no asyncio.debug() function. Debug mode can also be enabled with PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1, loop.set_debug(True) or development mode (-X dev), which then logs steps that block the loop for over 100 ms.

questions.text: A server holds thousands of mostly idle network connections and does little computation per request. Which model fits best?
options: One OS thread per connection
One process per connection
An asyncio event loop
A process pool sized to the CPU count
questions.explanation: Async tasks are much cheaper than threads or processes, and one event loop can wait on many sockets at once. CPU-heavy work would be better offloaded to workers.

questions.text: Compared with shared-memory systems, distributed-memory architectures are generally considered _____.
options: easier to program
more scalable
lower latency
less complex
questions.explanation: Adding nodes, each with its own memory, avoids a single shared memory bottleneck. The price is explicit communication over a network, which is slower and harder to program.

questions.text: Which scenario is the best fit for point-to-point communication?
options: A small number of specific tasks need to exchange data with each other
Every task must combine its value into one global sum at the end
One task must send the same data to every other task in the job
Every task must send distinct data to every other task
questions.explanation: Point-to-point operations such as MPI_Send and MPI_Recv connect one sender with one receiver. Patterns involving the whole group are better expressed with collectives.

questions.text: In MPI, what is a rank?
options: The operating-system PID of an MPI process
The scheduling priority MPI gives a process
The number of the CPU core a process runs on
A process's index within a communicator, starting at 0
questions.explanation: Ranks run from 0 to size minus 1 and are assigned per communicator, so the same process can have different ranks in different communicators. They are not OS process IDs.

questions.text: What is MPI_COMM_WORLD?
options: A communicator for talking to programs running outside the MPI job
A global variable shared by every process
The predefined communicator containing all processes started in the job
A function that creates new processes while the job is running
questions.explanation: After MPI_Init, every process belongs to MPI_COMM_WORLD. Programs can derive smaller communicators from it for subgroups.

questions.text: What does an MPI communicator combine?
options: A process group and a context that isolates its messages
A network socket and a buffer for each message
A process and the thread that sends its messages
A send buffer and a matching receive buffer
questions.explanation: The context guarantees that messages sent in one communicator cannot be received in another, which is why libraries often use their own duplicated communicator.

questions.text: Eight processes call MPI_Comm_split(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank / 4, rank, &new_comm), where rank is the world rank. What rank and size does world rank 6 see in new_comm?
options: Rank 6, size 8
Rank 0, size 4
Rank 1, size 2
Rank 2, size 4
questions.explanation: The color 6 / 4 = 1 groups it with world ranks 4-7, and the key orders that group by world rank, so it becomes rank 2 of 4. Ranks belong to a communicator, not to a process.

questions.text: An MPI program calls MPI_Comm_rank and MPI_Comm_size on MPI_COMM_WORLD and is launched with mpirun -np 4. What values do they report?
options: Ranks 1 to 4, and size 4
Ranks 0 to 3, and size 4
Ranks 0 to 4, and size 5
Every process reports rank 0, and size 4
questions.explanation: MPI_Comm_size gives the number of processes in the communicator. Each process gets a distinct rank starting from 0.

questions.text:
What does this launch command start?

mpiexec -n 1 ./manager : -n 4 ./worker
options: Five copies of manager, because only the first program is used
Two separate jobs, whose MPI_COMM_WORLD sizes are 1 and 4
One manager process that later spawns 4 worker processes itself
One job of 5 ranks running two programs, sharing one MPI_COMM_WORLD
questions.explanation: The colon separates the programs of one MPMD (multiple-program, multiple-data) launch. Launchers such as MPICH's and Open MPI's number ranks in the order given, so manager is rank 0 and the workers are ranks 1-4.

questions.text: What is the purpose of MPI_Finalize()?
options: To clean up the MPI environment after all MPI work is complete
To combine the final results from all processes
To send any final messages to the root process
To act as a barrier that guarantees all output is printed
questions.explanation: Every process calls it once at the end, after completing its communication. Most MPI calls are not allowed afterwards.

questions.text: When a blocking MPI_Send returns, what is guaranteed?
options: The receiver has received and processed the message
The send buffer can be safely reused
The matching receive has been posted
The message has been written to disk
questions.explanation: Standard-mode MPI_Send may return after copying the data into a system buffer or only after the receiver starts receiving. Either way, only buffer reuse is guaranteed.

questions.text: A process calls MPI_Isend on a buffer. When may it safely modify that buffer?
options: Immediately after MPI_Isend returns
After the receiving process calls MPI_Finalize
Once MPI_Wait or MPI_Test reports completion
Never, because the buffer belongs to MPI from then on
questions.explanation: A nonblocking send only starts the operation. Until the request completes, MPI may still be reading the buffer, so changing it could corrupt the message.

questions.text:
What is wrong with this code on the receiving rank?

MPI_Irecv(buf, n, MPI_DOUBLE, 0, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, &req);
printf("%f\n", buf[0]);
MPI_Wait(&req, MPI_STATUS_IGNORE);
options: Nothing, because MPI_Irecv fills buf before returning
MPI_Wait must be called before MPI_Irecv
It reads buf before the receive has completed
MPI_Irecv cannot receive MPI_DOUBLE data
questions.explanation: Until MPI_Wait or a successful MPI_Test completes the request, the buffer must not be accessed: it may still hold old or partly written data. Read buf after the wait.

questions.text: How does MPI_Test differ from MPI_Wait?
options: MPI_Test cancels the operation if it is not finished
MPI_Test sends a test message; MPI_Wait sends real data
MPI_Test works only for sends; MPI_Wait only for receives
MPI_Test checks without blocking; MPI_Wait blocks until done
questions.explanation: MPI_Test sets a flag and returns immediately, so a process can do other work and check again later. MPI_Wait is the blocking choice.

questions.text: When does a synchronous-mode send, MPI_Ssend, complete?
options: As soon as the data is copied into a system buffer
Only after the matching receive has started
Only after the receiver has finished processing the data
Immediately, like a nonblocking send
questions.explanation: MPI_Ssend never completes by buffering alone. Testing code with it reveals programs that only work because the implementation happens to buffer messages.

questions.text:
Two ranks each run the code below, with other set to the opposite rank. It completes with n = 1 but hangs with n = 1000000. Why?

MPI_Send(sendbuf, n, MPI_INT, other, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
MPI_Recv(recvbuf, n, MPI_INT, other, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, MPI_STATUS_IGNORE);
options: Small sends were buffered; large ones wait for receives that never start
MPI_Send rejects messages above a fixed size limit and retries forever
Large messages are split into parts that arrive out of order
MPI_Recv can receive only messages that fit in one network packet
questions.explanation: Standard-mode MPI_Send may buffer or may wait for the matching receive; implementations usually buffer only small messages. Each rank then waits in MPI_Send for the other, so the code is unsafe for every n.

questions.text: Two ranks must swap large buffers. Which version cannot deadlock, however much or little MPI buffers?
options: Each rank calls MPI_Send, then MPI_Recv
Each rank calls MPI_Recv, then MPI_Send
Each rank calls MPI_Isend, then MPI_Recv, then MPI_Wait
Each rank calls MPI_Ssend, then MPI_Recv
questions.explanation: The nonblocking send lets each rank reach its receive, so both transfers complete. Send-first relies on buffering, while MPI_Ssend-first and receive-first always deadlock. MPI_Sendrecv is another safe choice.

questions.text: What does MPI_Barrier(comm) guarantee?
options: No process leaves it until every process has entered it
Only one process at a time can send messages afterwards
All pending messages in the communicator are delivered
All processes print their output in rank order
questions.explanation: A barrier is an explicit synchronization point. It says nothing about message delivery and should not be used to patch an unclear communication design.

questions.text: Can a collective such as MPI_Bcast be relied on as a substitute for MPI_Barrier?
options: Yes, every collective synchronizes all processes like a barrier
No, because collectives can be called by only some processes
Yes, as long as the root process is rank 0
No, it may return before other processes have entered it
questions.explanation: Every process in the communicator must make the matching call, but only MPI_Barrier guarantees that all have arrived. A broadcast root, for example, may return as soon as its buffer can be reused.

questions.text: What is collective communication in MPI?
options: A message exchanged between exactly two processes
An operation every process in the communicator must call
Communication that uses shared memory instead of messages
Messages exchanged between two separate MPI jobs
questions.explanation: Collectives express group patterns directly, which makes intent clear and lets the implementation use efficient tree or ring algorithms.

questions.text: What does MPI_Bcast() do?
options: Copies the root's data to every process in the communicator
Broadcasts a message to every computer on the network
Sends a different piece of data to each process
Collects one value from every process at the root
questions.explanation: After the call, every process has a copy of the root's buffer. Scattering different pieces is MPI_Scatter.

questions.text: Four ranks hold the values 4, 7, 2 and 9 and call MPI_Reduce with MPI_SUM and root 0. What is the result?
options: Every rank receives 22
Each rank receives the sum of the values before it
Rank 0 receives 4, its own value
Rank 0 receives 22
questions.explanation: MPI_Reduce combines the values with the given operation and stores the result only at the root. MPI_Allreduce would give 22 to every rank.

questions.text: How does MPI_Allreduce differ from MPI_Reduce?
options: It works on all MPI data types, not only on integers
It is nonblocking, while MPI_Reduce is blocking
Every process receives the reduced result, not just the root
It reduces the data from every communicator in the job at once
questions.explanation: All-reduce is common when every process needs the global value, such as a convergence norm in a simulation or summed gradients in distributed training.

questions.text:
Every rank of an iterative solver runs the loop below. Why does it use MPI_Allreduce rather than MPI_Reduce to rank 0?

while (globalerr > tol) {
    exchange_halos();
    compute();
    localerr = max_local_error();
    MPI_Allreduce(&localerr, &globalerr, 1, MPI_FLOAT, MPI_MAX, comm);
}
options: MPI_Reduce cannot compute a maximum, only sums
Every rank needs globalerr to decide whether to continue
MPI_Allreduce needs no network communication
MPI_Reduce works only with integer data types
questions.explanation: With MPI_Reduce, only the root would see the new error. The other ranks would test a stale value and could leave the loop at a different iteration, mismatching later halo exchanges and collectives.

questions.text: What is the difference between MPI_Scatter and MPI_Gather?
options: Scatter is meant for small messages, while Gather is for large ones
Scatter is synchronous; Gather is asynchronous and returns early
Scatter sends the same data everywhere; Gather sums the data
Scatter splits root data among processes; Gather collects pieces at the root
questions.explanation: They are inverse patterns. A typical program scatters chunks of an array, lets each process work on its chunk, then gathers the results.

questions.text: The root must distribute 1,000 array elements as evenly as possible among 3 processes. Which collective fits?
options: MPI_Scatter, with a count of 333 for every process
MPI_Alltoall, with the root as the only sender
MPI_Scatterv, with per-process counts and displacements
MPI_Gather, with counts of 334, 333 and 333
questions.explanation: MPI_Scatter sends the same count to every process, and 1,000 is not divisible by 3. MPI_Scatterv accepts counts such as 334, 333 and 333 with matching displacements.

questions.text: What does MPI_Alltoall do?
options: Broadcasts one buffer from every process to the root
Every process sends a distinct block of data to every other process
Reduces data from all processes and broadcasts the result
Synchronizes all processes without exchanging data
questions.explanation: All-to-all is a complete exchange, used for example in distributed matrix transposes and FFTs. Its cost grows quickly with process count.

questions.text: Ranks 0-3 contribute the values 1, 2, 3 and 4 to MPI_Scan with MPI_SUM. What does rank 2 receive?
questions.explanation: MPI_Scan is an inclusive prefix reduction: rank $i$ receives the combination of values from ranks 0 to $i$. Rank 2 gets $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$; the exclusive MPI_Exscan would give 3.

questions.text: What are message tags used for in MPI?
options: Distinguishing kinds of messages between the same processes
Labelling messages so debuggers can display them
Selecting how the message's header is compressed in transit
Choosing the key used to encrypt the message
questions.explanation: A receive matches on communicator, source and tag. Distinct tags let a process receive, for example, data messages and control messages separately.

questions.text: An application and a library it calls both send messages on MPI_COMM_WORLD with tag 0. What can go wrong, and what is the usual fix?
options: A receive may match the other's message; the library should use MPI_Comm_dup
Tag 0 is reserved for libraries; the application must use tag 1
The library's messages are dropped; call MPI_Barrier before each library call
Nothing, because MPI matches messages by the calling function
questions.explanation: Matching uses only communicator, source and tag. A duplicated communicator has the same group but its own context, so library traffic can never match the application's receives.

questions.text: Rank 0 receives from ranks 1 and 2 with MPI_ANY_SOURCE. Why might the output differ between runs?
options: MPI_ANY_SOURCE drops one of the messages at random
MPI reorders the messages from each sender
MPI_ANY_SOURCE only works with blocking sends
Messages from different senders can arrive in either order
questions.explanation: Arrival order across senders depends on timing. Naming the expected source rank, and a specific tag, removes the ambiguity when the program needs a fixed order.

questions.text: In a ring, each rank sends to (rank + 1) % np. To receive deterministically instead of using MPI_ANY_SOURCE, which source should each rank name in C?
options: (rank + 1) % np
(rank - 1) % np
(rank - 1 + np) % np
rank
questions.explanation: Each rank's message comes from its left neighbor. Adding np first matters because in C, -1 % np is -1, which is not a valid rank for rank 0.

questions.text: Single-threaded rank 1 sends two messages to rank 0 with the same tag and communicator, and rank 0 posts two receives that match either. In what order does rank 0 receive them?
options: In any order, depending on network timing
In the order they were sent
Only the second one, which overwrites the first
In order of message size, smallest first
questions.explanation: MPI's non-overtaking rule: messages from one sender to one receiver that match the same receive arrive in send order. There is no ordering guarantee across different senders, or between sends made concurrently by several threads.

questions.text: Why might a process call MPI_Probe before MPI_Recv?
options: To check whether the network link is working
To learn an incoming message's size before allocating a buffer
To test whether the sending process is still alive
To measure the round-trip network latency to the sender
questions.explanation: MPI_Probe returns a status describing a matching message without receiving it. MPI_Get_count on that status gives its size, so the buffer can be allocated exactly.

questions.text: A receive specifies a count of 100 elements, but the matching message has 60. What happens?
options: MPI reports an error because the counts differ
The receive waits for 40 more elements
The remaining 40 elements are filled with zeros
It succeeds, and MPI_Get_count reports 60
questions.explanation: The receive count is a capacity, so it can exceed the message size. Receiving a message larger than the buffer is the error case, MPI_ERR_TRUNCATE.

questions.text: What is a Cartesian topology in MPI?
options: A virtual grid of processes, in 1D, 2D or 3D
The physical layout of cables in a cluster
A row-major memory layout for storing matrices
A visualisation produced by MPI debugging tools
questions.explanation: MPI_Cart_create builds the grid and MPI_Cart_shift finds neighbor ranks, which suits grid-based simulations; dimensions can be periodic. Virtual topologies do not move processes to other hardware.

questions.text: What is an intercommunicator, created for example with MPI_Intercomm_create?
options: A communicator limited to the processes on one node
A copy of a communicator that has a new context
A communicator connecting two disjoint groups of processes
A communicator whose ranks are arranged as a grid
questions.explanation: In point-to-point calls on an intercommunicator, ranks refer to the remote group, so, for example, a simulation group can send to an analysis group. A copy with a new context comes from MPI_Comm_dup.

questions.text: Why use an MPI derived datatype such as MPI_Type_vector to send a matrix column?
options: It compresses the column's data before sending it
It describes the strided layout, so no manual packing is needed
It transposes the column into a row on the receiving side
It is the only way MPI can send floating-point data
questions.explanation: In a row-major matrix, a column's elements are not contiguous. A vector type with the right stride lets MPI read them directly.

questions.text: What are ghost (halo) cells in a domain-decomposed simulation?
options: Cells that store data deleted during the simulation
Unused cells added to pad arrays to a power of two
Local copies of neighbors' boundary values
Cells that record errors detected during communication
questions.explanation: A stencil near the edge of a subdomain needs neighbor values. Each step, processes exchange their boundary data to refresh these halo copies.

questions.text: What is latency hiding in distributed computing?
options: Overlapping communication with independent computation
Hiding network delays from users with a progress bar
Compressing messages so they arrive sooner
Caching every remote value locally in advance
questions.explanation: A process can post nonblocking sends and receives, compute work that does not depend on them, and only then wait. Actual overlap depends on the MPI implementation making progress.

questions.text: What does the CAP theorem say about distributed data stores?
options: They can guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance at all times
Replication always reduces both consistency and availability
Caching, availability and performance cannot be optimised together
During a network partition, a system must choose between consistency and availability
questions.explanation: Partitions cannot be ruled out in real networks. While one lasts, a node must either refuse requests (keeping consistency) or answer with possibly stale data (keeping availability).

questions.text: What is eventual consistency?
options: Every read always returns the latest write
Data becomes consistent only after the whole system restarts
If updates stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value
Writes are applied to all replicas in one fixed global order
questions.explanation: Replicas may temporarily disagree, so a read can return stale data. Many highly available systems accept this in exchange for lower latency and partition tolerance.

questions.text: What is a primary trade-off of replicating data across nodes?
options: It improves availability and reads but makes consistency costlier
It always reduces the latency of every single write
It removes any need to handle node or link failures
It only benefits write-heavy workloads
questions.explanation: More copies mean more places to read from and survive failures, but every write must be propagated and conflicts resolved.

questions.text: What is sharding?
options: Copying the full dataset to every node
Caching data only at the network edge
Compressing data before it is stored on disk
Partitioning data so each node holds only a subset
questions.explanation: Each shard owns a range or hash of keys, so storage and writes scale out. Queries that span many shards become more expensive, so the shard key is chosen to keep common queries local.

questions.text: What makes failure handling fundamentally different in a distributed system than on a single machine?
options: Distributed systems never experience hardware failures
Partial failure: one node or link can fail while the rest keeps running
A failure on any node always stops the whole system immediately
Failures can only occur in the network, never in nodes
questions.explanation: A slow or silent node is hard to distinguish from a crashed one. Systems therefore use timeouts, retries, replication and checkpointing to keep working.

questions.text: How does a typical cluster differ from a general distributed system?
options: Its nodes are usually colocated and centrally managed
Its machines all share one physical memory
It cannot run tightly coupled MPI programs
It must consist of identical hardware nodes
questions.explanation: A cluster is a kind of distributed system. Its low-latency interconnect and shared scheduling make tightly coupled jobs such as MPI simulations practical, and heterogeneous CPU/GPU clusters are common.

questions.text: Flynn's taxonomy classifies computer architectures by the number of concurrent _ streams and ___ streams.
options: instruction; data
input; output
program; memory
cache; I/O
questions.explanation: Combining single or multiple instruction streams with single or multiple data streams gives the four classes SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD.

questions.text: In Flynn's taxonomy, which class describes a modern multicore PC across its cores?
options: SISD
SIMD
MISD
MIMD
questions.explanation: Each core runs its own instruction stream on its own data. Inside each core, vector instructions also provide SIMD, so real systems often combine classes.

questions.text: Which is a typical example of SIMD execution?
options: Two cores running unrelated programs
A cluster of nodes exchanging MPI messages
Redundant computers checking each other's results on the same input
One AVX instruction adding eight pairs of 32-bit floats at once
questions.explanation: SIMD applies one instruction to multiple data elements. CPU vector extensions such as SSE, AVX and NEON, and vector processors, are classic SIMD hardware.

questions.text: Which class in Flynn's taxonomy has no widely used general-purpose machines?
options: SISD
SIMD
MISD
MIMD
questions.explanation: Redundant fault-tolerant computation is sometimes cited as MISD, but pure MISD hardware is rare. The other classes describe scalar CPUs, vector units and multicore systems or clusters.

questions.text: A two-socket server has many cores per socket, each with AVX-512 vector units, and memory attached to each socket. Which description fits it?
options: MIMD across cores, SIMD within each core, and NUMA memory
UMA, because all of its cores share one address space
SIMD only, because its cores execute vector instructions
MISD, because several cores can read the same data
questions.explanation: These terms describe different dimensions, so one machine can be all three. A shared address space does not make access times uniform: each socket reaches its own memory faster than the other socket's.

questions.text: A Symmetric Multi-Processing (SMP) system has two or more _ processors connected to a single ___ main memory.
options: identical; distributed
dissimilar; shared
identical; shared
dissimilar; distributed
questions.explanation: In SMP all processors are equal peers with the same view of one shared memory, and any of them can run any thread.

questions.text: A CPU has 8 physical cores, each with 2-way simultaneous multithreading (SMT). How many logical CPUs does the OS see?
questions.explanation: Each SMT context appears to the OS as a logical CPU. The 16 contexts still share only 8 cores' execution units and caches.

questions.text: Compared with a processor that has 8 physical cores, a hyperthreaded processor with 8 logical cores (4 physical) usually provides _____ performance.
options: higher
lower
identical
double
questions.explanation: SMT threads share one core's execution units, caches and bandwidth. SMT improves utilisation when one thread stalls, but it does not match a second physical core.

questions.text: A program creates 64 threads on a machine with 4 logical CPUs. What does it get?
options: 64 threads executing instructions at the same instant
An error, because threads cannot outnumber logical CPUs
A 16-fold speedup over the same program with 4 threads
64 concurrent threads, but at most 4 running at any instant
questions.explanation: The OS time-slices the threads over the 4 hardware contexts. Source-level concurrency does not create hardware parallelism; extra threads can hide blocking I/O but only add switching overhead to CPU-bound work.

questions.text: In modern multicore CPUs, what normally keeps the cores' cached copies of memory consistent?
options: The application, by flushing its caches manually after writes
The operating system, during every context switch
The processor hardware, through a cache-coherence protocol
The compiler, by inserting copy instructions
questions.explanation: Coherence is maintained transparently by hardware, typically with a MESI-style protocol. Software sees one consistent value per cache line without managing copies itself.

questions.text: Under a MESI protocol, cores 0 and 1 both hold a cache line in the Shared state. Core 0 then writes to it. What happens?
options: Core 1's copy is invalidated, and core 0's becomes Modified
Core 1's copy is updated in place, and both stay Shared
The write goes straight to DRAM, and both copies stay Shared
Core 0 waits until core 1 evicts the line on its own
questions.explanation: MESI is a write-invalidate protocol: a core must hold the only valid copy before it writes. Core 1's next access misses and fetches the new value, which is the traffic that false sharing multiplies.

questions.text: Which of these applications would benefit most from parallel execution on multiple cores?
options: A tool that downloads several files from the Internet
A math library that processes large matrices
A logging service that frequently writes to a database
A GUI form for an accounting application
questions.explanation: Large matrix operations are CPU-bound and split naturally into independent pieces. The downloader and logger are mostly I/O-bound, so concurrency helps them more than parallel computation.

questions.text: What is a cache line?
options: The fixed-size block, often 64 bytes, that caches transfer
The bus that connects the L1 cache to main memory
A queue of pending requests waiting for the cache
A register that counts cache hits and misses
questions.explanation: Caches load and track whole lines, not individual bytes. This is why nearby data is cheap to access and why unrelated variables can share a line.

questions.text:
With N = 4096, the column-order loop below ran about 10 times slower than the row-order loop at gcc -O2. Why?

static double a[N][N];
for (i = 0; i < N; i++) for (j = 0; j < N; j++) s += a[i][j];   /* row order */
for (j = 0; j < N; j++) for (i = 0; i < N; i++) s += a[i][j];   /* column order */
options: The column-order loop performs more additions in total
The compiler runs only the row-order loop on several cores
C stores arrays column by column, so the names are swapped
Each column-order access touches a different cache line
questions.explanation: C arrays are row-major, so a[i][j] and a[i + 1][j] are 32 KiB apart. The row loop uses all eight doubles of each 64-byte line and streams well; the column loop uses one per line fetched.

questions.text: What is false sharing?
options: One thread reading memory that belongs to another process
Two threads reading invalid data because of a race
Threads writing separate variables on the same cache line
A security flaw that leaks cache contents across cores
questions.explanation: The variables are logically independent, but the cache line keeps moving between cores. False sharing can slow a program even when it has no data race.

questions.text: Each worker thread increments its own counter, but the counters sit next to each other in one array and the program scales poorly. What is a likely fix?
options: Protect all the counters with one mutex
Give each worker's counter its own cache line
Declare every counter as volatile
Add more worker threads to spread the load
questions.explanation: Adjacent counters share cache lines, so every increment invalidates other cores' copies. Padding them apart, or keeping local counts and combining them at the end, removes that traffic.

questions.text: Does hardware cache coherence make unsynchronized concurrent code correct?
options: Yes, coherence guarantees every thread sees writes in program order
No, ordering still needs atomics, locks or other synchronization
Yes, but only on x86 processors with strong ordering
No, because coherence is disabled when several threads run
questions.explanation: Coherence keeps each cache line consistent, but compilers and CPUs still reorder operations. The language memory model, through synchronization, is what defines correct ordering.

questions.text: How do UMA and NUMA architectures differ?
options: UMA access time is uniform; in NUMA it depends on location
NUMA systems cannot offer a shared address space
UMA is found only in single-core processors
NUMA uses faster memory chips than UMA systems
questions.explanation: In NUMA, memory is attached to particular sockets or nodes, and local accesses are faster than remote ones. Modern multi-socket servers are typically cache-coherent NUMA.

questions.text: On a Linux NUMA server, one thread initialises a large array and then 32 threads on two sockets process it. Why might the threads on one socket run slower?
options: NUMA prevents two sockets from reading the same array
The other socket's cores have a lower clock speed
First-touch placed every page on the initialising thread's node
Only one socket at a time can use its L1 caches
questions.explanation: By default a page lives on the node of the thread that first touches it, so the other socket's accesses are remote. Initialising data in parallel, with the same threads that will use it, keeps accesses local.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a memory barrier (fence)?
options: To protect memory from unauthorised access
To flush the entire CPU cache to disk
To allocate a new block of aligned memory
To limit how memory operations may be reordered
questions.explanation: A fence stops the compiler and CPU from reordering certain loads and stores across it. Atomics with acquire or release ordering provide the same kind of guarantee in a structured way.

questions.text: What is branch prediction?
options: The compiler choosing which branch of an if to compile
The CPU guessing a branch's outcome to keep fetching instructions
Predicting which memory addresses a program will access next
Running both sides of every branch on different cores
questions.explanation: A correct guess keeps the pipeline full. A misprediction forces the CPU to discard the speculative work and refill the pipeline, costing many cycles.

questions.text: What is speculative execution?
options: Executing instructions before knowing they are needed, undoing wrong guesses
A compiler optimisation that deletes code it predicts will be unused
A debugging mode that executes every instruction twice to check it
Running only the code the programmer marked as optional
questions.explanation: Combined with branch prediction, speculation lets the CPU work ahead. Only correctly predicted results are committed to the architectural state.

questions.text: What does out-of-order execution do?
options: Executes the program's statements in a random order each run
Executes instructions backwards to undo earlier mistakes
Reorders the source code once at compile time
Runs independent instructions as soon as their inputs are ready
questions.explanation: While one instruction waits, for example on a cache miss, later independent instructions can run. Retiring in order preserves the program's visible behavior on that core.

questions.text: What is instruction-level parallelism (ILP)?
options: Running several programs at once on several cores
Splitting one instruction across several cores
One core executing several independent instructions at once
Parallelism between different programming languages
questions.explanation: Pipelining, superscalar issue and out-of-order execution exploit ILP. Data dependencies between instructions limit how much is available.

questions.text: On a single-threaded workload, CPU A runs at 4 GHz and averages 1 instruction per cycle; CPU B runs at 3 GHz and averages 2. Both execute the same instructions. Which finishes first?
options: CPU B, at about 6 billion instructions per second
CPU A, at about 4 billion instructions per second
Neither, since clock speed and IPC cancel each other out
CPU A, since IPC does not affect how long a program runs
questions.explanation: Instruction throughput is clock rate times IPC: $4 \times 1 = 4$ versus $3 \times 2 = 6$ billion per second. Clock speed alone does not predict performance.

questions.text:
Compiled with gcc -O2 (no -ffast-math), the second loop below summed the same double array about 3.5 times faster than the first on a modern x86 CPU. Why?

for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    s += a[i];

for (i = 0; i < n; i += 4) {   /* n is a multiple of 4 */
    s0 += a[i]; s1 += a[i + 1]; s2 += a[i + 2]; s3 += a[i + 3];
}
options: The second loop uses integer additions instead of floating point
The second loop is automatically split across four CPU cores
The second loop reads a quarter as much memory as the first
Four independent dependency chains let the core overlap the additions
questions.explanation: Each s += a[i] waits for the previous addition's result, so the first loop is limited by floating-point add latency. The compiler may not reorder it itself, because floating-point addition is not associative.

questions.text: How do the L1, L2 and L3 caches typically compare?
options: They are the same size but store different kinds of data
L1 is shared by all cores, while L3 is private to each core
L1 is smallest and fastest; L3 is largest and slowest
L3 is fastest because it is closest to memory
questions.explanation: Each level trades speed for capacity, with L2 in between. L1 is usually private to a core, while L3 is often shared by several or all cores.

questions.text: What is a GPU's architecture optimised for?
options: Running operating-system code with low latency
High throughput on many similar, independent operations
Fast execution of single-threaded, branch-heavy programs
Managing file systems and storage devices
questions.explanation: A GPU keeps many lightweight threads in flight and switches between them to hide memory latency. CPUs invest more hardware in making a few threads fast.

questions.text: When can offloading a computation to a GPU make it slower than running it on the CPU?
options: Whenever the CPU has more than eight cores
Whenever the data is stored in floating point
When the problem is small and data transfers dominate
When the algorithm is perfectly data-parallel
questions.explanation: A GPU is not automatically faster. Transfer cost, small problem size, branch divergence and low arithmetic intensity can all remove the benefit.

questions.text: What does GPGPU computing mean?
options: Using a GPU only for rendering games and video
Using GPUs for general-purpose, non-graphics computation
A shading language for writing graphics effects
A tool for debugging graphics drivers on Linux
questions.explanation: Programming models such as CUDA, HIP, OpenCL and SYCL let GPUs run simulations, linear algebra and machine learning workloads.

questions.text: What best describes the difference between latency and throughput?
options: Latency is time per operation; throughput is work per unit time
Latency matters only for GPUs; throughput only for CPUs
Latency is work per second; throughput is the time for one operation
Both measure the same thing in different units
questions.explanation: A system can process many items per second while each item still takes a long time. CPUs lean towards low latency, GPUs towards high throughput.

questions.text: How are data parallelism and SIMD related?
options: They are two names for the same hardware feature
Data parallelism requires a GPU, while SIMD requires a cluster
SIMD is a workload property; data parallelism is a CPU instruction set
Data parallelism is a workload property; SIMD is one way to exploit it
questions.explanation: Applying the same operation to many elements can be executed with SIMD instructions, GPU threads in SIMT groups or multiple cores.

questions.text: What is a vector processor?
options: A processor whose instructions operate on whole vectors of elements
A processor with many independent, identical cores
A processor dedicated to drawing vector graphics on screen
A processor that only performs integer arithmetic
questions.explanation: One vector instruction streams many elements through deep pipelines, so a new element can enter every cycle after start-up. Long vectors use the hardware best.

questions.text: What is cache thrashing?
options: Deliberately clearing the cache to improve security
Repeated misses as data is evicted before it can be reused
Two caches exchanging lines faster than memory can
A cache optimisation that prefetches data in bulk
questions.explanation: Thrashing happens when the working set does not fit, or when access patterns map many addresses to the same cache sets. Performance then approaches that of main memory.

questions.text: How do shared-memory and distributed-memory systems differ?
options: Shared memory is used for small data; distributed memory for large data
Shared memory is always faster; distributed memory is always slower
Shared: one address space; distributed: per-node memory and messages
There is no practical difference for programmers
questions.explanation: Shared memory lets threads communicate through loads and stores. Distributed memory scales further but requires explicit message passing, for example with MPI.

questions.text: What is memory bandwidth?
options: The total amount of installed memory
The number of memory addresses a program may use
The delay before the first byte of a request arrives
The rate at which data can be read from or written to memory
questions.explanation: Bandwidth is measured in bytes per second and limits data-heavy workloads. The delay for one access is latency, a separate property.

questions.text: A memory-bound loop already saturates DRAM bandwidth with 8 cores. What usually happens if you run it on 16 cores?
options: It barely speeds up, since bandwidth is already saturated
It becomes about twice as fast, like compute-bound code
It always slows down to exactly half its speed
It becomes compute-bound and scales linearly
questions.explanation: All cores share finite memory bandwidth. Once it is saturated, extra cores add compute capacity that the loop cannot use.

questions.text: A compute-bound job whose threads share no data speeds up only about 6.5 times going from 1 to 8 cores of a desktop CPU. Which hardware effect is a plausible cause?
options: The cache line size shrinks as more cores become active
SIMD instructions are disabled when more than one core is active
The cores run at a lower clock frequency when all of them are busy
The CPU allows only one core at a time to execute arithmetic
questions.explanation: Turbo frequencies are highest with few active cores; power and thermal limits lower clocks when all are busy. Shared caches, memory bandwidth and SMT siblings are other common causes of sublinear scaling.

questions.text: What is hardware prefetching?
options: Loading a program into memory before it is started
Compiling frequently used functions ahead of time
Reordering data in memory so it is sorted
Loading data into cache before the program requests it
questions.explanation: Prefetchers recognise patterns such as sequential or strided access. Predictable access patterns therefore run much faster than random ones.

questions.text: What is the "memory wall"?
options: A physical limit on how much RAM a single machine can hold
The growing gap between processor speed and memory access speed
A hardware barrier that isolates each process's memory from others
A cache that blocks writes from reaching memory
questions.explanation: Processors improved faster than DRAM latency for decades, so many programs spend much of their time waiting for memory. Caches, prefetching and locality-aware code help.

questions.text: With a write-back cache policy, when is modified data written to main memory?
options: Immediately, as part of every store
When the dirty line is evicted or flushed
Only when the owning program exits
Never, because the cache replaces main memory
questions.explanation: Write-back avoids writing to memory on every store, saving bandwidth. A write-through cache, by contrast, updates memory on every write.

questions.text: Which of these describes a program's latency?
options: The ratio of sequential to parallel execution time
The number of processors the program uses
The number of tasks completed per unit of time
The time one task takes to complete
questions.explanation: Latency is measured per operation, from start to finish. Percentiles such as p95 and p99 are often reported because an average can hide slow outliers.

questions.text: A server is always busy processing exactly 4 requests at a time, and each request takes 200 ms. What is its throughput?
options: 5 requests per second
20 requests per second
200 requests per second
800 requests per second
questions.explanation: Each of the 4 slots completes $\frac{1}{0.2\,\text{s}} = 5$ requests per second, giving 20 in total. Latency is still 200 ms: concurrency raised throughput without making any single request faster.

questions.text: Which of these describes a program's speedup?
options: One-processor time divided by $p$-processor time
The number of processors the program uses
The number of tasks completed per unit of time
The time one task takes to complete
questions.explanation: Speedup is $S_p = \frac{T_1}{T_p}$, based on wall-clock time for the same problem. A speedup of $p$ is linear, or ideal, speedup.

questions.text: 85% of a program's runtime is parallelizable and runs 6 times faster on a 6-core processor. According to Amdahl's Law, what is the overall speedup?
options: About 3.43
About 4.62
About 5.10
Exactly 6.00
questions.explanation: $S = \frac{1}{(1 - 0.85) + \frac{0.85}{6}} = \frac{1}{0.15 + 0.142} \approx 3.43$. The 15% serial portion keeps the result well below the core count.

questions.text: Amdahl's Law gives a(n) _____ on the overall speedup from parallelizing a program.
options: exact prediction
lower limit
average value
upper limit
questions.explanation: The model assumes the parallel part divides perfectly and ignores communication, synchronization and imbalance. Real programs therefore usually do worse; superlinear cache effects are an exception, because they change the per-processor work the model assumes.

questions.text: If 95% of a fixed-size program can be parallelized, what is the maximum speedup with unlimited processors, according to Amdahl's Law?
questions.explanation: As the processor count grows, the speedup approaches $\frac{1}{1 - P} = \frac{1}{0.05} = 20$. The 5% serial part takes the same time no matter how many processors are added.

questions.text: 95% of a fixed-size program's runtime is perfectly parallelizable. According to Amdahl's Law, how many processors are needed for a speedup of 10?
questions.explanation: Solve $\frac{1}{0.05 + 0.95/n} = 10$: then $0.05 + \frac{0.95}{n} = 0.1$, so $n = 19$. Reaching half of the limit of 20 already takes 19 processors.

questions.text: A function accounts for 10% of a program's runtime. If it were made infinitely fast, what is the best possible overall speedup?
options: About 1.11
About 1.9
Unlimited
questions.explanation: By Amdahl's Law, the other 90% is unchanged, so the speedup is at most $\frac{1}{0.9} \approx 1.11$. Optimization effort belongs where the measured runtime is.

questions.text: How does Gustafson's Law differ from Amdahl's Law?
options: It applies only to shared-memory machines
It gives a lower bound instead of an upper bound
It assumes the serial fraction grows with $p$
It lets the problem grow with the processor count
questions.explanation: Amdahl asks how much faster a fixed problem can run. Gustafson asks how much larger a problem can be solved in about the same time, giving a more optimistic, weak-scaling view.

questions.text: A scaled workload has a serial fraction of 0.05. What speedup does Gustafson's Law predict on 32 processors?
options: About 12.5
About 20.0
About 30.45
Exactly 32.0
questions.explanation: Gustafson's scaled speedup is $p - \alpha(p - 1) = 32 - 0.05 \times 31 = 30.45$. Because the parallel work grows with $p$, the serial part matters much less than under Amdahl's Law.

questions.text: With a serial fraction of 0.1 on 8 processors, Amdahl's Law predicts a speedup of about 4.7 but Gustafson's Law predicts 7.3. Why is this not a contradiction?
options: Gustafson's Law ignores the serial part of the program entirely
Gustafson's fraction is measured on a run whose problem grows with $p$
Amdahl's Law applies only to distributed-memory machines
Gustafson's Law assumes the processors run at a higher clock speed
questions.explanation: Amdahl gives $\frac{1}{0.1 + 0.9/8} \approx 4.71$ for a fixed problem. Gustafson gives $8 - 0.1 \times 7 = 7.3$, where 0.1 is the serial share of the larger, scaled parallel run. They answer different questions.

questions.text: A computation takes 100 seconds on one processor and 28 seconds on four. What is its parallel efficiency?
options: About 28%
About 72%
About 89%
About 357%
questions.explanation: Speedup is $\frac{100}{28} \approx 3.57$, and efficiency is speedup divided by processor count: $\frac{3.57}{4} \approx 0.89$. An efficiency near 100% means near-linear speedup.

questions.text: As more processors are applied to a fixed-size problem, what typically happens to parallel efficiency?
options: It falls, even while speedup may still increase
It rises steadily along with speedup
It becomes exactly zero beyond 8 processors
It stays constant at 100%
questions.explanation: Serial work, communication and synchronization stay roughly constant or grow while each processor's share of useful work shrinks, so each added processor contributes less.

questions.text: What is superlinear speedup, and what can cause it?
options: An impossible result that always indicates a timing bug
Speedup below 1, caused by too much communication
Speedup exactly equal to $p$, from perfect load balance
Speedup above $p$, often because each part now fits in cache
questions.explanation: Splitting the problem shrinks each worker's working set, which can cut cache misses or paging. The parallel run then does less memory work per element than the one-processor baseline.

questions.text: What is an advantage of fine-grained parallelism with many small tasks?
options: A high computation-to-communication ratio
Lower scheduling overhead
Better cache locality
Good load balancing
questions.explanation: Many small tasks can be spread evenly and rebalanced dynamically. The cost is more frequent scheduling, synchronization and communication.

questions.text: What is an advantage of coarse-grained parallelism with a few large tasks?
options: Good load balancing for irregular work
A high computation-to-communication ratio
More tasks available than processors
Easier recovery from slow tasks
questions.explanation: Large tasks do more computation between coordination events, so overhead is a smaller fraction of runtime. If a few tasks run long, though, other processors sit idle.

questions.text: Granularity can be described as the ratio of _ to ___.
options: computation; communication
speedup; number of processors
tasks; number of processors
tasks; time
questions.explanation: Granularity compares useful work in a task with its coordination cost. A task must do enough work to amortise the cost of scheduling and communicating it.

questions.text: In a computational graph, which of these describes the critical path?
options: The longest chain of dependent operations through the program
The total time of all task nodes in the graph
The shortest path from the start node to the end node
The set of tasks that access shared memory
questions.explanation: Operations on the critical path must run one after another, so its length bounds the execution time no matter how many processors are available.

questions.text: Task A (2 s) must finish before tasks B (3 s) and C (5 s) can start, and task D (1 s) needs both B and C. What are the work and span?
options: Work 11 s, span 6 s
Work 11 s, span 8 s
Work 8 s, span 11 s
Work 11 s, span 11 s
questions.explanation: Work sums every task: $2 + 3 + 5 + 1 = 11$ s. Span is the longest dependency path, A, C, D: $2 + 5 + 1 = 8$ s. The parallelism, $\frac{11}{8} \approx 1.4$, caps the speedup however many processors are used.

questions.text: In a computational graph, which of these describes a program's span?
options: The total time of all task nodes in the graph
The time between the first and second task nodes
The number of processors needed to run the graph
The total time of the task nodes along the critical path
questions.explanation: Span, $T_\infty$, is the execution time with unlimited processors. It equals the length of the critical path.

questions.text: What does the ratio of work to span represent?
options: The communication overhead paid per processor
The parallelism, an upper bound on achievable speedup
The fraction of the program that must run serially
The number of tasks that are on the critical path
questions.explanation: Because span is part of the work, the ratio is always at least 1. A ratio of 1 means no parallelism; larger values mean more processors can be used profitably.

questions.text: A computation has work $T_1 = 1000$ s and span $T_\infty = 50$ s. What lower bound do the work and span laws give for its runtime on 8 processors?
questions.explanation: $T_p \ge \max\left(\frac{T_1}{p}, T_\infty\right) = \max(125, 50) = 125$ s. A greedy scheduler needs at most $\frac{T_1}{p} + T_\infty = 175$ s.

questions.text: Why are computational graphs useful when designing a parallel program?
options: They show which tasks depend on which, exposing parallelism
They automatically eliminate data races between tasks
They replace the need to measure performance later
They pinpoint exactly which lines of code need a mutex
questions.explanation: Tasks with no path between them in the graph are independent and can run concurrently. The graph also exposes the critical path that limits speedup.

questions.text: Increasing the number of processors while keeping the problem size per processor fixed (weak scaling) aims to accomplish _ in ___.
options: the same work; less time
less work; the same time
more work; less time
more work; the same time
questions.explanation: In weak scaling the total problem grows with the machine. Ideally the runtime stays constant while the total amount of work increases.

questions.text: Increasing the number of processors while keeping the total problem size fixed (strong scaling) aims to accomplish _ in ___.
options: more work; less time
the same work; less time
more work; the same time
less work; more time
questions.explanation: Strong scaling divides a fixed problem among more processors. It eventually saturates when each processor's share becomes too small relative to overhead.
