questions.text: In a weak-scaling study, one unit of work takes 10 s on 1 processor, and 64 units take 12.5 s on 64 processors. What is the weak-scaling efficiency $E_{\text{weak}} = \frac{T_1}{T_p}$?
options: About 1.3%
questions.explanation: $\frac{10}{12.5} = 0.8$. In ideal weak scaling the runtime stays constant as work and processors grow together, giving an efficiency of 1.

questions.text: A parallel code on 1 thread runs twice as slowly as the best sequential program. On 8 threads it runs 6 times faster than on 1 thread. What is its speedup over the best sequential program?
questions.explanation: $T_{\text{par}}(1) = 2T_s$, so $T_{\text{par}}(8) = \frac{2T_s}{6} = \frac{T_s}{3}$. Reporting only the relative speedup of 6 would hide the parallel version's overhead, so always state the baseline.

questions.text: Why should you repeat a timing measurement several times and report the variation?
options: The system clock drifts randomly between runs
The first run always crashes on parallel machines
Scheduling, caches and background load vary between runs
Averaging makes the program itself run faster
questions.explanation: Scheduling, cache state, frequency scaling and background activity all change runtimes. Repeated runs, with warm-up handled consistently, show typical behavior and how much it varies.

questions.text: A report compares a serial run's end-to-end time, including loading the input, with a parallel run's compute-phase time only. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as both runs use the same input data
A compute phase cannot be timed inside a parallel program
Serial programs must always be timed using CPU time
The timed regions differ, so the reported speedup is inflated
questions.explanation: The comparison credits parallelism with removing input loading that it never sped up. Time the same region in both runs, and report excluded startup or transfers separately.

questions.text: A parallel run on 4 processors takes 30 seconds, and the one-processor baseline takes 100 seconds. What is the total parallel overhead, $T_o = p \cdot T_p - T_1$?
options: 0 seconds
20 seconds
70 seconds
120 seconds
questions.explanation: The parallel run consumes $4 \times 30 = 120$ processor-seconds, while the useful work is 100 seconds. The extra 20 seconds are communication, synchronization, idle time and other overhead.

questions.text: What does the scalability of a parallel program describe?
options: How its performance changes as resources are added
The maximum number of threads its language allows
How large its source code can grow over time
How many users can download and install it at once
questions.explanation: A scalable program keeps gaining useful performance as resources grow. Scalability is measured experimentally, for example with strong- and weak-scaling studies.

questions.text: What is load imbalance?
options: Uneven work, so some processors wait while others are busy
Too much total work for the machine's memory to hold
A power supply that cannot sustain the processors' load
A network link carrying more traffic than another
questions.explanation: In synchronized programs the slowest worker sets the runtime. Dynamic scheduling, work stealing or finer-grained tasks can improve balance.

questions.text: Four workers finish a phase in 10, 10, 10 and 30 seconds. What is the imbalance ratio, $T_{\max} / T_{\text{avg}}$?
questions.explanation: The average is $\frac{60}{4} = 15$ seconds, and $\frac{30}{15} = 2.0$. A ratio of 1.0 would mean perfect balance; here three workers sit idle for 20 seconds each.

questions.text: What does isoefficiency describe?
options: Every processor in a system having equal efficiency
The efficiency of a program's reads and writes to disk
The energy used per operation by a parallel computer
How fast problem size must grow with $p$ to keep efficiency fixed
questions.explanation: A slowly growing isoefficiency function means the algorithm scales well: modest increases in problem size keep added processors productive.

questions.text: A program uses 4 threads and finishes in 10 seconds of elapsed time, consuming about 40 seconds of CPU time. Which time should be used to compute its speedup?
options: The CPU time of the slowest thread only
The 40 seconds of CPU time
The 10 seconds of wall-clock time
The CPU time divided by the number of threads
questions.explanation: Speedup is about how long the user waits, which is elapsed wall-clock time. CPU time adds up across threads and can increase even as the program gets faster.

questions.text: Why do larger problems often achieve better parallel speedup than small ones?
options: Larger problems always contain less serial code
Fixed overheads become a smaller share of the total work
Larger problems run at a higher clock frequency
Small problems cannot be split across processors at all
questions.explanation: Communication and start-up costs matter relatively less as useful work per processor grows. This is the effect Gustafson's Law and weak scaling describe.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of profiling a parallel program?
options: To find where time goes, including waiting, before optimising
To list every hardware platform the program supports
To test the program for security vulnerabilities
To create performance profiles for different users
questions.explanation: In parallel programs, time is often lost in locks, barriers, communication or imbalance rather than in the hottest function. Measure first, then optimise the measured bottleneck.

questions.text: Dashboards show a cluster job's throughput dropping every night at 02:00. What is the usual next step?
options: Add more nodes, since monitoring has already found the cause
Profile or trace the job during that period to find out why
Stop monitoring the job, since collecting metrics adds overhead
Raise the alert threshold so the nightly drop no longer alerts
questions.explanation: Monitoring shows when and where a problem occurs; profiling and tracing the affected phase explain why, for example a competing backup job or one slow node.

questions.text: How does sampling profiling differ from instrumentation?
options: Sampling requires recompiling the whole program; instrumentation never does
They are two names for the same profiling technique
Sampling can measure only GPU code; instrumentation only CPU code
Sampling records the location periodically; instrumentation adds measurement code
questions.explanation: Tools such as perf sample, which barely disturbs timing. Instrumentation, such as the call counting gprof adds with -pg or Callgrind's binary instrumentation, records every call but can change the behavior it measures.

questions.text: What does the roofline model show?
options: The network topology connecting the nodes of a cluster
The physical height limit of racks in a data centre
Performance bounds set by peak compute and memory bandwidth
The cost of a machine relative to its performance
questions.explanation: It plots attainable performance against arithmetic intensity. Kernels with low intensity sit under the sloped memory-bandwidth roof; those with high intensity hit the flat compute roof. It shows which limit to attack.

questions.text: What is arithmetic intensity?
options: Operations performed per byte moved from memory
How complicated a program's mathematical formulas are
The clock speed of the arithmetic units
The number of arithmetic units in a processor
questions.explanation: High arithmetic intensity means each byte loaded is reused for much computation, so the code is more likely to be compute-bound than memory-bound.

questions.text: When timing an MPI phase, why is the maximum elapsed time across ranks reported, for example with MPI_Reduce and MPI_MAX?
options: The maximum is always the most accurate single measurement
Rank 0 cannot measure its own time
The phase is not complete until the slowest rank finishes
MPI timers only work on the slowest rank
questions.explanation: Averaging per-rank times would hide stragglers. The parallel phase ends when every rank has finished, so the slowest one determines its duration.

questions.text: A program reports 100% CPU utilisation on every core but shows poor speedup. How is this possible?
options: It is not possible, since full utilisation guarantees linear speedup
Speedup cannot be measured when utilisation is 100%
Utilisation counters are always inaccurate on multicore CPUs
Cores may be busy spinning on locks, missing in cache or redoing work
questions.explanation: Busy is not the same as productive. Interpret utilisation together with throughput, efficiency and hardware counters to see whether the cycles are doing useful work.

questions.text: Why can timing only the host call that launches a GPU kernel be misleading?
options: Kernel launches always take exactly the same time as the kernel
The launch returns before the kernel finishes running
GPU kernels cannot be timed from the host at all
The host clock is paused while a kernel runs
questions.explanation: The timer captures only submission. Use GPU events for device time, or synchronize before stopping a host timer. Also state whether data transfers and allocation are included.

questions.text: In a strong-scaling study, what is the "scaling knee"?
options: The processor count at which the program first produces correct output
The point where efficiency first exceeds 100%
The processor count at which power consumption is highest
The point beyond which adding processors gives little further improvement
questions.explanation: Plotting runtime, speedup and efficiency against processor count shows where gains flatten out. Running past the knee wastes resources for that workload and configuration.

questions.text: What are the four stages of Foster's PCAM parallel design methodology?
options: Planning, Coding, Analysis, Monitoring
Partitioning, Combination, Assignment, Measurement
Preparation, Computation, Aggregation, Merging
Partitioning, Communication, Agglomeration, Mapping
questions.explanation: Partitioning splits the work into tasks, communication identifies the data they exchange, agglomeration groups tasks, and mapping assigns them to processors.

questions.text: Which stage of the parallel design process focuses on breaking the problem down into discrete pieces of work?
options: Partitioning
Agglomeration
Communication
Mapping
questions.explanation: Partitioning exposes the available parallelism, ideally producing many more potential tasks than processors so later stages have flexibility.

questions.text: Which stage of the parallel design process focuses on what data tasks must exchange and how they coordinate?
options: Communication
Agglomeration
Partitioning
Mapping
questions.explanation: The communication stage identifies which tasks need each other's results and how they exchange them, distinguishing data movement from synchronization.

questions.text: A heat solver first gives one 512×512 block to each of 64 ranks, then is redesigned so that each of 16 ranks owns a 2×2 group of those blocks. Which PCAM stage is this change?
options: Partitioning
Communication
Agglomeration
Mapping
questions.explanation: Merging neighboring tasks into larger units cuts the number of ranks and messages and raises the interior-to-boundary ratio. Sixteen tiles still leave enough units to spread across the machine.

questions.text: You decide which node and which cores each of 16 MPI ranks runs on, placing ranks that exchange halos on the same node. Which PCAM stage is this?
options: Communication
Partitioning
Mapping
Agglomeration
questions.explanation: Mapping assigns tasks to cores, sockets, nodes or accelerators to balance load and keep frequently communicating tasks close together. The tasks themselves are already fixed by the earlier stages.

questions.text: Why does the partitioning stage come before the communication stage?
options: Tasks must be grouped into larger units first
The order of the four stages is arbitrary
Each task's physical location must be known first
The division of work determines what data must be exchanged
questions.explanation: Communication needs depend on the dependencies between the tasks produced by partitioning. Grouping happens later, in agglomeration, and placement in mapping.

questions.text: How should the PCAM stages be applied in practice?
options: Strictly once and in order, never revisiting an earlier stage
Iteratively, revisiting earlier stages when later ones expose problems
In any order, since the stages do not affect each other
Only the mapping stage is still needed on modern hardware
questions.explanation: For example, a mapping may reveal that communication is too costly, prompting different agglomeration or partitioning. The final design should be validated by measurement.

questions.text: Why do programmers often skip explicit mapping for threads on a typical desktop operating system?
options: The OS scheduler assigns threads to cores automatically
Desktop computers have too few cores for mapping to matter
Desktop operating systems forbid choosing a thread's core
Mapping only applies to GPU programs
questions.explanation: The scheduler places and migrates threads dynamically. Affinity and pinning can still matter for performance, especially on NUMA or HPC systems.

questions.text: What is domain decomposition?
options: Dividing a problem by the different operations it performs
Splitting a program into modules by business domain
Dividing the data into chunks that workers process alike
Separating the problem domain from the solution domain
questions.explanation: Each worker owns a region of the data. It works well when computation is mostly local, as in image filters, simulations and matrix operations.

questions.text: A 2D grid is split among four workers. Why do $2 \times 2$ square tiles usually communicate less than four thin strips?
options: Tiles have less boundary per area, so less halo exchange
Square tiles contain fewer grid points in total
Thin strips cannot be processed in parallel at all
Square tiles never need any ghost cells
questions.explanation: Computation grows with a tile's area, while communication grows with its perimeter. For an $N \times N$ grid, the cuts total $2N$ for tiles but $3N$ for strips.

questions.text: In a 2-D stencil, the side of a square tile doubles from $L$ to $2L$. How do its per-step computation and halo volume change?
options: Both double
Both grow 4 times
Computation grows 4 times, halo volume 2 times
Computation grows 2 times, halo volume 4 times
questions.explanation: Work grows with the area, $L^2$, and boundary data with the perimeter, $L$. Larger tiles do more computation per halo element, but too few tiles leave too little parallel work.

questions.text: Each rank owns a $1024 \times 1024$ tile of double values and, every step, sends one boundary row or column to each of its 4 neighbors. How much halo data does it send per step?
options: 4,096 bytes
8,192 bytes
32,768 bytes
questions.explanation: One edge is $1024 \times 8 = 8192$ bytes, and four edges give 32,768 bytes, about 32 KiB. The tile itself is $1024^2 \times 8$ bytes, 8 MiB, so the halos are a small fraction of the data.

questions.text: What is functional decomposition?
options: Splitting functions into smaller helper functions
Dividing a dataset into equal contiguous blocks
Removing unused functions to shrink the program
Dividing a problem by the different operations it performs
questions.explanation: For example, a web request can pass through authentication, database, formatting and rendering stages, each handled by its own workers. This naturally forms pipelines.

questions.text: A three-stage pipeline takes 2 ms, 5 ms and 3 ms per item, with one worker per stage. What is its steady-state throughput?
options: 100 items per second
200 items per second
333 items per second
500 items per second
questions.explanation: Once the pipeline is full, the slowest stage completes one item every 5 ms, so throughput is 200 items per second. Each item's latency is still 10 ms.

questions.text: A three-stage pipeline takes 2 ms, 5 ms and 3 ms per item, with one worker per stage. A second worker is added to the 5 ms stage. What is the new steady-state throughput?
options: 200 items per second
About 333 items per second
400 items per second
500 items per second
questions.explanation: Two workers finish middle-stage items every 2.5 ms on average, so the 3 ms stage becomes the bottleneck: $\frac{1000}{3} \approx 333$ items per second. Doubling the slowest stage did not double throughput.

questions.text: What is the difference between data parallelism and task parallelism?
options: Data parallelism is always faster than task parallelism on CPUs
Data: same operation on different data; task: different operations at once
Task parallelism always uses more memory than data parallelism
Data parallelism applies only to database queries
questions.explanation: An image filter applied to every pixel is data-parallel; serving unrelated requests or running pipeline stages at once is task-parallel. Real programs often combine both.

questions.text: What is an embarrassingly parallel computation?
options: A computation too simple to be worth parallelizing
A computation that always contains hidden race conditions
One made of independent tasks needing little or no communication
A poorly designed algorithm that parallelizes badly in practice
questions.explanation: Rendering separate frames or running independent Monte Carlo trials are examples. Such workloads usually scale well, limited mainly by load balance and I/O.

questions.text: What does a divide-and-conquer algorithm do when it reaches the base case?
options: Merges all of the subproblems created so far
Stops subdividing and solves the subproblem directly
Recursively solves a set of smaller subproblems
Divides the problem into two smaller subproblems
questions.explanation: The base case ends the recursion. In parallel versions, a cutoff on problem size also stops creating tasks too small to be worth scheduling.

questions.text: What is the master-worker (manager-worker) pattern?
options: One process hands out tasks to workers and collects results
Every process does identical work with no coordination
Workers elect a new master every time a task finishes
A pattern used only for handling errors in workers
questions.explanation: The master hands out tasks and gathers results, which balances load naturally. With many workers, the master itself can become a bottleneck.

questions.text: What is the bag-of-tasks (work queue) pattern?
options: Running every task on every worker for redundancy
Giving every worker a fixed list of tasks up front
Storing completed results in an unordered collection
Workers repeatedly take the next task from a shared pool
questions.explanation: Load balances dynamically: fast workers simply take more tasks, so uneven task costs balance out. Contention on the shared queue can limit scaling with many workers.

questions.text: What is work stealing?
options: Idle workers take tasks from the queues of busy workers
A scheduler that cancels slow tasks and restarts them elsewhere
A security attack in which a process takes another's CPU time
A type of race condition in task queues
questions.explanation: Each worker mostly uses its own deque, so there is no central bottleneck. Only idle workers steal, which keeps contention low while balancing load.

questions.text: How does static load balancing differ from dynamic load balancing?
options: Static is meant for unchanging data; dynamic is for data that changes
Static is always faster, while dynamic is always more accurate
Static assigns work up front; dynamic reassigns it during execution
Static uses threads; dynamic uses processes
questions.explanation: Static mapping has no run-time overhead and suits uniform, predictable work. Dynamic mapping handles irregular task costs but adds scheduling overhead and may reduce locality.

questions.text: What is the fork-join model?
options: A model for committing database transactions
A task splits into parallel subtasks, then waits for all of them
A pattern in which child processes duplicate the parent's open files
A network protocol for joining new nodes to a running cluster
questions.explanation: Parallel regions open and close around independent work, as in OpenMP parallel loops or recursive parallel merge sort.

questions.text: What is the SPMD (Single Program, Multiple Data) model?
options: Each processor runs a different program on the same data
A hardware design in which one instruction controls all cores
One processor runs the program while others store data
Every processor runs the same program on different data
questions.explanation: Most MPI programs are SPMD: every rank runs the same executable and uses its rank to select its portion of the data or role.

questions.text: What is speculative parallelism?
options: Running parallel algorithms that have not been tested
Doing work in parallel before knowing whether it is needed
Assigning tasks to processors at random to save time
Estimating a program's speedup without running it
questions.explanation: For example, both branches of a costly decision can be computed while the condition is evaluated. Unneeded results are discarded, trading extra work for lower latency.

questions.text: What characterises the bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) model?
options: Processes communicate continuously without synchronizing
All data is processed in one large batch on a single processor
Supersteps of local computation, communication and a barrier
A hardware architecture built around one shared bus
questions.explanation: Within a superstep, processes compute on local data and send messages. The barrier at the end makes the messages available for the next superstep.

questions.text: Which loop cannot be parallelized by simply splitting its iterations among threads?
options: for i in range(n): c[i] = a[i] + b[i]
for i in range(n): c[i] = max(a[i], b[i])
for i in range(n): b[i] = 2 * a[i]
for i in range(1, n): a[i] = a[i - 1] + b[i]
questions.explanation: Each iteration needs the result of the previous one, a loop-carried dependency. The others are independent per index; this one needs a restructured algorithm such as a parallel scan.

questions.text: What is a stencil computation?
options: Updating each grid element from a fixed pattern of its neighbors
A protocol for broadcasting data from one root
A tool for drawing a program's task dependency graph
A code template that new parallel programs are written from
questions.explanation: Heat diffusion and image blurs are stencils. In parallel versions, each worker needs halo data from neighbors at its boundaries every step.

questions.text: What is a reduction in parallel computing?
options: Reducing the number of processors to save power
Combining many values into one, using an operation like sum
Simplifying parallel code by removing all its locks
Reducing a program's peak memory usage by compression
questions.explanation: The operation, such as sum or max, must be associative. Workers compute partial results locally, then combine them, typically in a tree, which takes logarithmic steps instead of a serial loop.

questions.text: What does a prefix sum (scan) compute for the input [3, 1, 4, 2]?
questions.explanation: An inclusive scan gives the running total at every position. It can be computed in parallel and is a building block for many parallel algorithms.

questions.text: Why does data locality matter in parallel design?
options: It keeps data stored in local files rather than databases
It is a security measure that hides data from other processes
Using nearby data cuts communication and memory traffic
It guarantees that no synchronization is needed
questions.explanation: Accessing nearby data is far cheaper than fetching it from another core's cache, another NUMA node or another machine. Good partitioning and mapping keep most accesses local.

questions.text: What does the "owner computes" rule state?
options: The owner of each piece of data computes its updates
The processor that compiled the code must execute it
Only the master process may write the final results
Every processor computes every value and compares results
questions.explanation: Assigning computation by data ownership keeps writes local and makes clear which process must send or receive boundary values.

questions.text: In a task dependency graph, what do the edges represent?
options: The physical links between processors
The memory each task allocates
Data or ordering dependencies between tasks
The order in which the programmer wrote the tasks
questions.explanation: Tasks without a path between them can run concurrently. The longest path, the critical path, limits the minimum execution time.

questions.text: What is block decomposition of an array?
options: Splitting source code into separate compilation blocks
Giving each worker one or more contiguous chunks of the array
Assigning individual elements to workers in round-robin order
Blocking all workers until the array is ready
questions.explanation: Contiguous blocks give good cache locality and simple index arithmetic. They balance poorly when some regions are much more expensive to process than others.

questions.text: With cyclic decomposition, item $i$ goes to worker $i \bmod P$. With 4 workers, which worker processes item 10?
options: Worker 0
Worker 1
Worker 2
Worker 3
questions.explanation: $10 \bmod 4 = 2$. Round-robin assignment spreads expensive items across workers, improving balance at the cost of locality.

questions.text: $C = AB$, with each matrix split into $2 \times 2$ blocks. Which formula gives the block $C_{11}$?
questions.explanation: Blocks multiply like scalar entries: block row 1 of $A$ times block column 1 of $B$. Each block product can reuse an optimized kernel on a cache-sized piece, while $A_{11}B_{12} + A_{12}B_{22}$ is $C_{12}$.

questions.text: Why is block-cyclic decomposition often used in distributed dense linear algebra?
options: It eliminates all communication between processes
It assigns the whole matrix to the fastest process
It needs no knowledge of the matrix dimensions
It balances load while keeping locality within blocks
questions.explanation: Blocks are dealt round-robin. Pure block layouts can leave some processes idle as the active region shrinks, and pure cyclic layouts lose locality. Block-cyclic is a compromise between the two.

questions.text: Message time is often modelled as $\alpha + n/B$ (startup latency plus size over bandwidth). What does this suggest about sending 1,000 tiny messages?
options: It costs the same as one message with the same total bytes
Latency is paid 1,000 times, so batching them is usually faster
Small messages are always faster because they use less bandwidth
Only the bandwidth term matters for small messages
questions.explanation: For small messages the fixed latency term dominates. Batching data reduces the number of startups paid, which is why agglomeration reduces communication cost.

questions.text: What is the goal of graph partitioning when mapping irregular tasks?
options: To balance work while cutting few communication edges
To give every partition the same number of edges
To place each task on its own separate processor
To remove all dependencies from the task graph
questions.explanation: Each cut edge represents communication between processors. Partitioners for meshes and sparse matrices balance the work per part while keeping cuts small.

questions.text: A stencil code uses nonblocking communication to overlap halo exchange with work. Which order of steps achieves this?
options: Wait for the halos, then post receives, then compute every point
Post receives, wait on them at once, then send the boundary data out
Post receives and sends, compute interior, wait, compute boundary
Compute the boundary, then the interior, and finally post receives
questions.explanation: Interior points do not depend on halo data, so they can be computed while messages are in flight. Only the boundary update must wait for the received values.

questions.text: A stencil code switches to MPI_Isend/MPI_Irecv and computes the interior before MPI_Waitall, but its runtime does not improve. A trace shows the data moving only inside MPI_Waitall. What is a likely cause?
options: Computing the interior corrupted the pending send buffers
Nonblocking calls are always slower than the matching blocking calls
MPI made little progress on the transfers during the computation
MPI_Waitall sends every message a second time to check it
questions.explanation: Nonblocking calls make overlap possible but do not guarantee it; many implementations advance large transfers only inside MPI calls. Occasional MPI_Test calls or asynchronous-progress settings can help, and the gain must be measured.

questions.text: A Jacobi solver keeps two arrays, A and B: it computes new values into B from A, then swaps them. Why not update A in place?
options: A single array cannot be shared by several OpenMP threads
Some neighbors would already hold new-step values when they are read
Two arrays halve the memory traffic of each time step
MPI cannot exchange halos from an array that is being updated
questions.explanation: A Jacobi step computes every value from the previous step only. In place, the result mixes old and new values, which changes the method, and in parallel it would depend on thread timing.

questions.text: A $4 \times 4$ grid of ranks R0-R15, numbered row by row, is placed four per node: R0-R3 on node A, R4-R7 on node B, and so on. With non-periodic boundaries, which halo exchanges cross between nodes?
options: North-south exchanges only
East-west exchanges only
Both directions, equally often
None, because each node holds whole rows
questions.explanation: East-west neighbors such as R1 and R2 share a node, while north-south neighbors such as R1 and R5 do not. Mapping decides which exchanges pay network cost.

questions.text: A hybrid job starts 16 MPI ranks with OMP_NUM_THREADS=8, but the launcher binds each rank to a single core. What is the likely result?
options: The MPI launcher rejects the job as invalid
OpenMP moves 7 of the threads to idle cores
Each rank still gets 8 cores, since OpenMP ignores binding
Each rank's 8 threads time-share one core
questions.explanation: Threads inherit their rank's CPU set, so all 8 compete for one core while others sit idle. Reserve 8 cores per rank, for example with Open MPI's --map-by ppr:4:node:PE=8, and check with --report-bindings.

questions.text: One design has 64 processing elements that each apply the same instruction to a different element in the same cycle. Another feeds elements one per cycle through a single deeply pipelined unit. Which pairing is correct?
options: The first is temporal parallelism; the second is spatial parallelism
The first is spatial parallelism; the second is temporal parallelism
Both are temporal parallelism, because both repeat one instruction
Both are spatial parallelism, because both process many elements
questions.explanation: Replicating processing elements that work side by side is spatial parallelism (an array processor). Reusing pipelined hardware over successive cycles is temporal parallelism (a vector pipeline). GPUs combine both.

questions.text: A float matrix with 4 rows and 6 columns is stored in row-major order. A loop walks down column 2. How many elements apart in memory are consecutive accesses?
questions.explanation: In row-major order the element below A(i,j) is one full row later, so the stride equals the number of columns, here 6. Walking along a row has stride 1.

questions.text: A matrix with 5 rows and 7 columns is stored row-major in a flat array starting at index 0. At which index is A(2,3)?
questions.explanation: The flat index is row * cols + col, so $2 \cdot 7 + 3 = 17$. Multiplying by the row count instead gives 13, and swapping row and column gives 23.

questions.text: A kernel stores particles as an array of struct { float x, y, z; } and thread i reads only particles[i].x. Why might converting to separate x[], y[] and z[] arrays speed it up?
options: Neighbouring threads then read neighbouring x values, so fewer memory transactions are needed
Separate arrays are stored in shared memory automatically instead of global memory
The compiler can only vectorise arrays of primitive types, never structures
Structures are padded to 64 bytes on GPUs, so each read fetches a whole cache line
questions.explanation: With the array of structures, consecutive threads read addresses 12 bytes apart and fetch y and z they do not use. A structure of arrays puts the x values contiguously, so a warp's loads coalesce.

questions.text: Which loop cannot be mapped directly to one GPU thread per iteration without changing its result?
options: for (i = 0; i < n; ++i) C[i] = A[i] + B[i];
for (i = 0; i < n; ++i) C[i] = 2 * A[i];
for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) C[i] = C[i - 1] + A[i];
for (i = 0; i < n; ++i) C[i] = (A[i] + B[i]) / 2;
questions.explanation: Each C[i] depends on C[i - 1] from the previous iteration, a loop-carried dependency. The other loops write each output from independent inputs, so their iterations can run in any order.

questions.text:
Compiled with GCC on x86-64, what does this C program print?

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    int a = -1, b = -2;
    printf("%d %d\n", (a + b) / 2, (a + b) >> 1);
    return 0;
}
options: -1 -1
-2 -2
-2 -1
-1 -2
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates towards zero, so $-3 / 2 = -1$. GCC implements >> on a negative int as an arithmetic shift, which rounds towards negative infinity, giving -2. Shifting is not a drop-in replacement for halving signed values.

questions.text: What does SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) mean for the programmer?
options: They write explicit vector instructions whose width matches the hardware lanes
They write scalar per-thread code, and the hardware runs threads in groups (warps)
Every thread runs on its own independent core with its own instruction fetch unit
Each thread executes a different kernel, chosen by its thread index
questions.explanation: In SIMT each thread has its own logical control flow and indices, while the hardware issues instructions for a warp or wavefront across its active lanes. Explicit vector width is the SIMD style, such as AVX.

questions.text: A CUDA block is one-dimensional with 256 threads. On an NVIDIA GPU, which warp and lane does the thread with threadIdx.x == 70 occupy?
options: Warp 1, lane 38
Warp 2, lane 70
Warp 3, lane 6
Warp 2, lane 6
questions.explanation: A block is split into warps of 32 threads with consecutive thread IDs, starting with thread 0 in warp 0. So $70 / 32 = 2$ (integer division) and $70 \bmod 32 = 6$.

questions.text: A CUDA block has blockDim = (16, 16, 1). Which warp contains the thread with threadIdx.x == 5 and threadIdx.y == 3?
options: Warp 1
Warp 0
Warp 3
Warp 5
questions.explanation: CUDA linearises the thread ID as x + y * blockDim.x, so this thread is $5 + 3 \cdot 16 = 53$. Warps hold IDs 0–31, 32–63 and so on, so ID 53 is in warp 1.

questions.text: A kernel is launched with 100 threads per block on an NVIDIA GPU. How many warps does each block occupy?
options: 3, and the remaining 4 threads are dropped
3, and the remaining 4 threads join the next block's warp
4, with only 4 active threads in the last warp
100, one warp per thread
questions.explanation: Warps are allocated in units of 32 threads, so 100 threads need $\lceil 100 / 32 \rceil = 4$ warps. The last warp has 28 inactive lanes, which is why block sizes are usually multiples of 32.

questions.text: A kernel uses 256-thread blocks. Which branch condition causes no divergence within any warp?
options: if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0)
if (threadIdx.x < 48)
if (threadIdx.x % 32 < 16)
if ((threadIdx.x / 32) % 2 == 0)
questions.explanation: threadIdx.x / 32 is the same for every thread in a warp, so each warp takes one path. The other conditions split warps: odd and even lanes, warp 1 at thread 48, or lower and upper half-lanes.

questions.text: Threads in a warp take both sides of an if/else. What does the hardware typically do?
options: It moves the threads that took the else path into a different warp for that branch
It runs each path in turn with the lanes not on that path masked off, then reconverges
It runs only the path taken by the majority of lanes and discards the others
It aborts the kernel with a divergence error
questions.explanation: Warps are fixed groups of threads and are not regrouped on divergence. The paths are serialised with an active mask, so the warp spends time on both paths and lane utilisation drops.

questions.text: A warp issues a load from global memory that takes hundreds of cycles. What does the SM scheduler usually do meanwhile?
options: It saves the warp's registers to memory and loads another warp, like an OS context switch
It idles the SM until the load returns, because warps run in a fixed order
It moves the stalled warp to a different SM that has the data cached
It issues instructions from other resident warps that are ready to run
questions.explanation: GPUs use fine-grained multithreading: many warps stay resident with their registers on chip, so switching between them costs almost nothing. Keeping enough ready warps is how GPUs hide memory latency.

questions.text: An SM has 65,536 registers and supports at most 64 resident warps. A kernel uses 64 registers per thread and 256-thread blocks. Ignoring allocation granularity and other limits, what occupancy does the register limit allow?
questions.explanation: One block needs $64 \cdot 256 = 16{,}384$ registers, so 4 blocks fit. That is 1,024 threads, or 32 warps, out of a maximum of 64 warps.

questions.text: You cut a kernel's register use so occupancy rises from 25% to 50%, but the kernel gets slower. What is a plausible reason?
options: Higher occupancy always increases branch divergence
Doubling occupancy halves the number of threads in each warp
Values now spill to local memory or are recomputed, adding slow memory traffic
The GPU throttles its clock whenever occupancy exceeds a fixed threshold
questions.explanation: Occupancy only measures resident warps relative to the maximum. If fewer registers force spills to local memory, which lives in device memory, or reduce data reuse, the extra traffic can outweigh the latency hiding.

questions.text: A 1D kernel computes int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;. What is i for the thread with blockIdx.x == 3, blockDim.x == 128 and threadIdx.x == 5?
questions.explanation: $3 \cdot 128 + 5 = 389$. Blocks 0, 1 and 2 cover indices 0–383, so block 3 starts at 384. The value 136 adds instead of multiplying the block terms.

questions.text: With n = 1000 and block = 256, the host computes grid = (n + block - 1) / block. How many launched threads fail the kernel's if (i < n) check?
questions.explanation: The grid is $(1000 + 255) / 256 = 4$ blocks, which is 1,024 threads. Threads 1,000–1,023 are past the end, so without the bounds check those 24 threads would access invalid memory.

questions.text: A host program uses grid = n / block; with n = 1000 and block = 256. What happens?
options: The launch fails because n is not a multiple of block
The runtime rounds the grid up, so every element is processed
Only 3 blocks run, so the last 232 elements are never processed
The last block runs with 232 threads instead of 256
questions.explanation: Integer division gives 3 blocks covering indices 0–767. The launch succeeds and leaves elements 768–999 untouched. Rounding up with (n + block - 1) / block plus a bounds check fixes it.

questions.text: A 2D kernel uses col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y and idx = row * width + col. With blockDim = (16, 16), blockIdx = (2, 1), threadIdx = (3, 4) and width = 100, what is idx?
questions.explanation: col is $2 \cdot 16 + 3 = 35$ and row is $1 \cdot 16 + 4 = 20$, so idx is $20 \cdot 100 + 35 = 2035$. The value 3520 swaps the roles of row and column.

questions.text: A kernel processes a row-major matrix with col derived from threadIdx.x and row from threadIdx.y. Which access pattern lets a warp's global loads coalesce best?
options: M[col * width + row]
M[row * width + col]
M[(row + col) * width]
M[col * width * width + row]
questions.explanation: Neighbouring threads in a warp differ in threadIdx.x, hence in col. With row * width + col they read consecutive addresses; with col * width + row they read addresses width elements apart.

questions.text:
A kernel uses a grid-stride loop and is launched with 2 blocks of 4 threads and n = 20. Which elements does the thread with global index 5 process?

for (int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; i < n;
     i += blockDim.x * gridDim.x) {
    out[i] = 2 * in[i];
}
options: 5 only
5 and 13
questions.explanation: The stride is the total thread count, $4 \cdot 2 = 8$, so the thread handles 5 and 13; the next value, 21, fails i < n. A grid-stride loop lets a fixed-size grid cover any n.

questions.text: A host program launches kernel<<<1, 2048>>>(...) on a current NVIDIA GPU. What happens?
options: The runtime splits the block into two blocks of 1,024 threads
The launch fails with a configuration error and the kernel does not run
The kernel runs with 2,048 threads but only 1,024 can use __syncthreads()
The kernel runs, with each hardware thread executing two logical threads
questions.explanation: On current GPUs a thread block may contain at most 1,024 threads. An invalid launch configuration is reported as an error, for example by cudaGetLastError(), and nothing is executed.

questions.text:
A program times a kernel like this. Why is the printed time misleading?

auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
myKernel<<<grid, block>>>(d_data, n);
auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
options: steady_clock cannot be called from a file compiled by nvcc
The first launch always includes copying the input to the GPU
Kernel launches are asynchronous, so it measures only the launch, not the execution
The kernel runs twice, once for each now() call
questions.explanation: The launch returns to the host before the kernel finishes. Synchronise before reading t1, or record cudaEvent_t start and stop events in the stream and use cudaEventElapsedTime().

questions.text: In the legacy default stream, the host launches a kernel and then calls cudaMemcpy(h, d, bytes, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost). Does it need cudaDeviceSynchronize() between them to read correct results?
options: No, the copy follows the kernel in the same stream and blocks until done
Yes, otherwise the copy may start while the kernel is still writing d
Yes, because cudaMemcpy returns before the copy has even started
No, because a kernel finishes before its launch call returns
questions.explanation: Work in one stream executes in issue order, and cudaMemcpy is synchronous with respect to the host. An explicit synchronisation is still useful for catching kernel errors close to their source.

questions.text: A kernel launch is followed by cudaGetLastError(), which returns cudaSuccess. Why might a later cudaDeviceSynchronize() still return an error?
options: cudaGetLastError() only reports errors from memory allocation calls
It reports launch errors, but faults during execution surface only once the kernel has run
cudaDeviceSynchronize() reports an error whenever more than one kernel was launched
cudaGetLastError() always returns cudaSuccess the first time it is called
questions.explanation: Because launches are asynchronous, an invalid memory access inside the kernel happens after the launch call returns. Checking the return value of a later synchronising call catches these execution errors.

questions.text: A kernel declares __shared__ float tile[256];. Who can read and write tile?
options: Every thread in the grid, through one copy per SM
The host, after the kernel completes, via cudaMemcpy
Only the single thread that declared it
All threads of the same block, each block having its own copy
questions.explanation: Shared memory is allocated per block and lives for the block's lifetime. Threads in other blocks see their own copy, and the host cannot access it directly.

questions.text: A kernel's local array is too large for registers and is placed in "local memory". Where does local memory physically reside?
options: In device memory, like global memory, cached in L1/L2
In the SM's register file
In the host's RAM, reached over PCIe
In the constant cache, since it is private to one thread
questions.explanation: "Local" describes per-thread scope, not location. Local memory and register spills live in device memory, so heavy use adds global-memory-like latency and traffic.

questions.text: Which data suits CUDA __constant__ memory best?
options: A 200 MB lookup table that every thread updates in place
Per-block scratch space that threads write and then read back
An output array in which each thread writes its own result
Small read-only coefficients that a warp's threads all read at one index
questions.explanation: Constant memory is small (typically 64 KB), read-only to kernels and cached. It works best when a warp's threads read the same address; scattered addresses within a warp are serialised.

questions.text: How are the L1 and L2 caches organised on a typical NVIDIA GPU?
options: Each SM has its own L1, and one L2 is shared by all SMs
Each warp has its own L1, and each block has its own L2
There is one L1 for the GPU, and each SM has a private L2
L1 and L2 are both in host memory and cache PCIe transfers
questions.explanation: L1 sits inside each SM (on many architectures sharing storage with shared memory), while L2 sits in front of the memory controllers and serves all SMs.

questions.text: Shared memory has 32 banks, and successive 32-bit words map to successive banks. Each thread of a warp reads s[threadIdx.x * 32] from a float array. What happens?
options: No conflict, because each thread reads a different address
A 2-way bank conflict
A 32-way bank conflict, because every address maps to bank 0
The hardware broadcasts one value to all 32 threads
questions.explanation: Word index 32 * t modulo 32 is always 0, so all 32 different addresses fall in one bank and are serialised. Broadcast applies only when threads read the same word.

questions.text: Under the same 32-bank layout, every thread of a warp reads s[0]. Is this a bank conflict?
options: No, the word is broadcast to all requesting threads
Yes, a 32-way conflict, since all threads use bank 0
Yes, a 2-way conflict between the two half-warps
It depends on whether s was declared volatile
questions.explanation: Conflicts arise when threads access different words in the same bank. When they read the same 32-bit word, the hardware broadcasts it, so the read is served in one pass.

questions.text: A transpose kernel declares __shared__ float tile[32][33]; instead of tile[32][32]. Why the extra column?
options: It stores a per-row checksum
It aligns each row to a 128-byte cache line
It leaves room for the __syncthreads() barrier counter
It shifts each row by one bank, so reading a column hits 32 different banks
questions.explanation: With 32 columns, tile[t][c] for different t all map to the same bank, giving a 32-way conflict on column reads. With 33 columns, row t starts one bank later, so the column spreads over all banks.

questions.text: In a 256-thread block, a kernel calls __syncthreads() inside if (threadIdx.x < 128) { ... }. What does CUDA guarantee?
options: The barrier synchronises only the 128 threads that enter the branch
The compiler moves the barrier outside the branch automatically
No defined behaviour: the program may hang or give wrong results
The other 128 threads wait at the end of the kernel instead
questions.explanation: __syncthreads() is allowed in conditional code only if the condition evaluates identically across the whole block. Otherwise behaviour is undefined, so keep the barrier outside the divergent branch.

questions.text: In the note's blockSum kernel, why is there a __syncthreads() between buf[t] = ... and the reduction loop?
options: It flushes buf to global memory so the host can read it
Threads then read buf[t + stride], which another thread wrote
It makes the 8 warps of the block execute in order
It is needed only when n is not a multiple of the block size
questions.explanation: Without the barrier, a thread could read a neighbour's slot before that thread has stored its input. The barrier makes every store in the block visible before any thread starts reading.

questions.text: The blockSum reduction halves stride from blockDim.x / 2 down to 1. What goes wrong if it is launched with blockDim.x == 192?
options: The loop never ends, because 192 is not a power of two
The kernel deadlocks at the first __syncthreads()
Thread 0 reads past the end of the shared-memory buffer
Some values are never added in, so the partial sum is wrong
questions.explanation: The strides become 96, 48, 24, 12, 6, 3, 1. At stride 3, buf[2] gets buf[5], but at stride 1 only buf[1] is added to buf[0], so buf[2] is lost. The halving scheme assumes a power-of-two block size.

questions.text: After blockSum writes one partial sum per block, you need the total. Why not have block 0 wait in the same kernel until all other blocks finish?
options: Blocks are not guaranteed to run concurrently or in any order, so waiting can deadlock
__syncthreads() already waits for all blocks, so the wait is redundant
Block 0 cannot read global memory written by other blocks
Partial sums are stored in shared memory and vanish when the kernel ends
questions.explanation: If block 0 spins while occupying an SM, a block it waits for may never be scheduled. Common fixes are a second kernel in the same stream, atomics, or a grid-wide sync with cooperative groups where supported.

questions.text: Many threads run bins[v] += 1; on a global histogram, and the counts come out too low. What is the standard fix?
options: Use atomicAdd(&bins[v], 1)
Put __syncthreads() before the increment
Declare bins as __constant__
Launch the kernel with one thread per bin
questions.explanation: The increment is a read-modify-write, so concurrent updates to the same bin overwrite each other. atomicAdd makes each update indivisible; __syncthreads() only orders threads of one block and does not prevent the race.

questions.text: Each thread runs int slot = atomicAdd(&count, 1); out[slot] = value; with count starting at 0. What does slot hold?
options: The new value of count, so the first thread gets 1
Always 0, because the atomic result is only visible after the kernel ends
An unspecified value unless the threads are in the same warp
The old value of count, so each thread gets a distinct index
questions.explanation: atomicAdd returns the value stored before the addition. Each thread receives a unique slot from 0 upwards, though the order in which threads get them is unspecified.

questions.text: Every thread in a large grid does atomicAdd(&total, x[i]) on one global variable, and the kernel is slow. What is a common improvement?
options: Reduce within each block in shared memory first, then do one atomic per block
Replace the atomic with a plain total += x[i], which is equivalent on GPUs
Move total into __constant__ memory so reads are cached
Add __syncthreads() after every atomic to spread them out
questions.explanation: Atomics to one address are serialised, so millions of them form a bottleneck. A block-level reduction cuts the global atomics to one per block.

questions.text: Why is host memory from cudaMallocHost() (pinned memory) used for cudaMemcpyAsync()?
options: It is allocated in GPU memory, so no transfer is needed at all
The GPU can DMA from page-locked pages, which truly async copies require
Pageable memory cannot be copied to the GPU at all
Pinned memory is the only kind that cudaFree() can release
questions.explanation: The GPU's copy engine needs host pages that cannot be moved or swapped. Pinned memory is necessary for truly asynchronous transfers and often copies faster, but pinning too much can hurt overall system performance.

questions.text: A program splits its data into chunks and issues copy-in, kernel and copy-out for each chunk in its own non-default stream, using pinned host buffers. What can this achieve?
options: It guarantees every chunk finishes in the order its stream was created
It removes the need to copy data between host and device
It lets operations within one stream run out of order
Copies for one chunk can overlap with kernels for another chunk
questions.explanation: Operations in one stream run in order, but different streams may overlap, so transfer time can hide behind computation. How much overlap occurs depends on the GPU's copy engines and resources.

questions.text: A program issues work to streams s1 and s2, both created with default flags, and also launches a kernel in the legacy default stream. What is the effect of that default-stream kernel?
options: It runs concurrently with everything, since the default stream has highest priority
It waits for earlier work in s1 and s2, and later work in them waits for it
It is rejected, because a program cannot mix default and non-default streams
It affects only work issued from other host processes
questions.explanation: The legacy default stream synchronises implicitly with blocking streams in the same context, which can serialise an overlapped pipeline. Non-blocking streams or the per-thread default stream avoid this.

questions.text: Which call is not allowed by CUDA's function execution-space qualifiers?
options: A __global__ kernel launched from host code with <<<grid, block>>>
Host code calling a __device__ function directly
A __global__ kernel calling a __device__ helper
Host code calling a __host__ __device__ function
questions.explanation: A __device__ function runs on the GPU and can be called only from device code. Marking a function __host__ __device__ compiles it for both sides, so host and kernels can both call it.

questions.text: An OpenCL kernel is being ported to CUDA. Which pair of terms corresponds most closely?
options: OpenCL work-group and CUDA warp
OpenCL __global memory and CUDA __shared__ memory
OpenCL __local memory and CUDA __shared__ memory
OpenCL work-item and CUDA block
questions.explanation: OpenCL __local memory is shared by the work-items of one work-group, just as CUDA __shared__ memory is shared by the threads of one block. A work-item maps to a thread and a work-group to a block.

questions.text: Why should code meant to run on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs avoid hard-coding a group width of 32?
options: NVIDIA warps grow to 64 threads when a block exceeds 512 threads
The width is chosen at random by the driver at each launch
Group width affects only graphics shaders, not compute kernels
AMD wavefronts are 64 or 32 lanes, depending on architecture and mode
questions.explanation: NVIDIA warps have 32 threads, but AMD wavefront width varies (wave64 on GCN and CDNA, wave32 or wave64 on RDNA). Querying the width, for example via warpSize, keeps warp-level code portable.
